blocks.text:
Every Java program you will ever read is built from classes. A class is a blueprint that bundles data (fields) with the operations on that data (methods), and an object is one concrete thing made from that blueprint. This sounds simple, and it is, until the day a bug turns out to be "two variables pointed at the same object" or "a field was read before it was assigned". Both bugs come from not having an accurate mental picture of what the JVM does when you write `new`. This chapter builds that picture, including the exact order in which Java initialises a class and its objects.

### State, behaviour and identity

An object has three things: **state** (the values stored in its fields), **behaviour** (the methods that read or change that state) and **identity** (it is this object and not another one that happens to hold the same values). Identity is the part beginners forget. Two `Book` objects with the same title and page count are still two objects; `==` on two references compares identity, not content.

A class declares what every object of that type has:

blocks.title: Book.java

blocks.text:
The fields `title` and `pagesRead` exist once per object. The methods exist once per class: the JVM does not copy method code into every object. When you call `book.read(10)`, the JVM passes `book` to the method as a hidden first argument, which is what the keyword `this` refers to inside it.

### References versus objects

When you write `Book b = new Book("Dune");` two different things happen. The `new` expression allocates an object on the **heap** and returns where it lives. The variable `b` is a **reference**: a small value (typically 4 or 8 bytes) that lets the JVM find the object. A local variable like `b` lives in the stack frame of the running method; the object it refers to lives on the heap. Copying a reference copies the arrow, never the object.
The next program makes this concrete. Read it first and predict the output of each line.

blocks.title: Refs.java

blocks.code:
$ java Refs.java
a.count = 5
a == b: true
a == c: false
after bump: 6
after replace: 6
NPE caught
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
What to notice. Changing `b.count` changed what `a` sees, because there is only one object. `a == c` is false although both hold 5, because `==` compares references. `bump` changed the caller's object, but `replace` did not: Java passes the *reference by value*. The method received its own copy of the arrow, repointed that copy at a brand new object, and the caller's arrow was untouched. "Java is pass-by-value, and for objects the value is a reference" is the exact, correct statement (Part 2 covers methods in more detail).

#### null and NullPointerException

A reference can hold `null`, meaning "no object". Using a null reference to reach a field or call a method throws `NullPointerException` (NPE). Since Java 14 the message says which expression was null, for example `Cannot invoke` `"String.length()" because "s" is null`; the variable name appears when the class was compiled with `javac -g` (otherwise you see `<local3>`). Primitives (`int`, `double`) can never be null; only references can.

#### When does an object die?

There is no `delete`. An object becomes eligible for garbage collection when no live reference can reach it any more. In `Object a = new Object(); Object b = a; a = null;` the object is still reachable through `b`, so it stays. Part 9 explains how the collector decides.

### Constructors

A **constructor** is code that runs when `new` creates an object, before the reference is returned to you. It has the class name and no return type. Its job is to put the object into a valid state. If you write no constructor at all, the compiler adds a public no-argument **default constructor**; the moment you write any constructor, that free one disappears.

Constructors can call each other with `this(...)`, which avoids duplicating validation:

blocks.title: Ctors.java

blocks.code:
$ java Ctors.java
Untitled (100 pages)
Dune (100 pages)
Dune (612 pages)
0 false null 0.0
pages must be positive: 0
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
What to notice. Only one constructor contains real logic; the others funnel into it. A `this(...)` call must be the first statement of the constructor (Java 25 relaxes this: code that does not touch `this` may precede it; see Part 11). The class `Empty` shows the **default values** the JVM gives *fields* before any code runs: `0` for numeric types, `false` for `boolean`, `'\u0000'` for `char`, `null` for references. **Local variables get no default**; the compiler refuses to compile a read of an unassigned local.

#### The keyword this

Inside an instance method or constructor, `this` is the reference to the current object. You need it in two situations: to tell a field from a parameter of the same name (`this.title = title`), and to pass the current object to another method. A constructor that fails by throwing leaves no usable object: the `new` expression never completes.

### Initialisation order

An object does not appear fully formed. Java runs a precise sequence, and getting it wrong causes some of the most confusing bugs: a method called from a superclass constructor that sees a field as `null`. The sequence has two phases.

**Class initialisation** happens once per class, the first time the class is actively used (first `new`, first call of a static method, first access to a non-constant static field). The JVM first initialises the superclass, then runs the class's `static` field initialisers and `static { }` blocks, in the order they appear in the source.

**Instance initialisation** happens for every `new`. Memory is allocated and zeroed (all fields get their default values), then the constructor runs in this order: the call to the superclass constructor first (`super(...)`, implicit if you wrote none); then the class's instance field initialisers and instance initialiser blocks `{ }` in source order; then the rest of the constructor body. The same rule applies at every level of the hierarchy, from `Object` downwards.

3 Base field initialiser
4 Base instance block
5 Base constructor

What to notice. The static blocks ran once, superclass first, and not on the second `new`. The line `Derived.show` `name=null y=0` is the trap: `Base`'s constructor called `show()`, which is overridden, so the **Derived** version ran while `Derived`'s field initialisers had not yet executed. It saw `name` as `null` and `y` as `0`, the zeroed defaults, even though `name` is assigned `"set"` in the source. The rule: never call an overridable method from a constructor.

You can see the mechanism in the bytecode. `javap -c -p 'InitOrder$Derived'` (trimmed) shows that the compiler copied the field initialisers and the instance block *into the constructor*, right after the call to the superclass constructor, and gathered the static block into a method called `static {}` (the class initialiser, `<clinit>`):

blocks.text:
#### Constants do not trigger class initialisation

A `static final` field whose value is a compile-time constant (a literal or constant expression of a primitive or `String`) is inlined by the compiler into every user. Reading it does not initialise the class at all:

blocks.title: Lazy.java

blocks.code:
$ java Lazy.java
MAX = 10
before NAME
Config initialised
NAME = name
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text: `MAX` printed without "Config initialised" appearing; reading `NAME` forced the class to initialise first. This laziness is also what makes the "initialisation on demand holder" singleton idiom in Part 12 work.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Never call an overridable method from a constructor. The subclass override runs before the subclass's own fields are initialised, so it reads defaults (`null`, `0`). Make the method `private`, `static` or `final`, or move the work out of the constructor into a factory method or an explicit `init()` step.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Field initialisers run in source order, and that order matters. `int a = b + 1; int b = 5;` does not compile (illegal forward reference), but `int a = getB() + 1; int b = 5;` does, and `a` ends up as 1 because `getB()` ran while `b` was still 0.

### Putting it together: a small class design

A well-formed class keeps its fields `private`, sets every field exactly once in a constructor that validates its input, and exposes only the operations callers need. Mark fields `final` whenever the value never changes after construction; the compiler then guarantees it is assigned exactly once, and the JVM guarantees other threads see it correctly (Part 8). Prefer a constructor that produces a fully valid object over a no-argument constructor followed by a chain of setters, because the latter lets other code observe a half-built object.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between a class and an object, and where do they live in memory? A class is a type definition (loaded once into the JVM, its metadata in Metaspace); an object is an instance created with `new`, allocated on the heap. A reference variable holds the address of the object, not the object, and the reference itself lives in a stack frame (local variable) or inside another object (field).

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: In what order do static blocks, instance blocks, field initialisers and constructors run? Superclass static initialisation, then subclass static initialisation (once per class). For each `new`: superclass constructor chain first (its field initialisers and instance blocks in source order, then its constructor body), then the subclass's initialisers and blocks, then the subclass constructor body.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Objects live on the heap; variables hold references. Assignment copies the reference, `==` compares identity.

- Fields get default values (`0`, `false`, `null`); locals do not.
- Order: superclass static, subclass static (once); then per object: super constructor, field initialisers and blocks in source order, constructor body.
- The compiler copies instance initialisers into each constructor after `super(...)`; static ones go to `<clinit>`.
- Do not call overridable methods from constructors; prefer final fields and constructors that fully validate.

The previous chapter treated every field as belonging to an object. Some data and behaviour belong to the class as a whole instead: a counter of how many accounts have been opened, a constant, a utility function like `Math.max`. The keyword `static` expresses that. A second, equally important question is who is allowed to touch what. Access modifiers and packages let a class hide its internals so they can change later without breaking its users. Together these two ideas are the foundation of encapsulation.

### Static members

A `static` field exists once per class, shared by all instances (and usable with no instance at all). A `static` method belongs to the class and has no `this`. Static members are accessed with the class name: `Account.issued()`.

blocks.title: Statics.java

blocks.code:
$ java Statics.java
1000 1001 issued=2
30.0
insufficient funds
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
What to notice. `nextId` is shared, so each constructor call hands out the next number. `id` is per object and `final`. A static method cannot read instance fields directly (there is no object), but an instance method can freely read static fields. The reverse mistake, calling an instance method from `static void main`, is the first compile error most beginners meet: `main` has no object, so you must create one first.

#### Static initialisers and constants

Constants are written `static final` with UPPER\_SNAKE\_CASE names. A static field that holds a mutable object (`static` `final List<String> NAMES = new ArrayList<>()`) is only a constant reference; the list can still change. Use `List.of(...)` or `Collections.unmodifiableList` for a genuinely fixed collection. Complex static setup goes in a `static { }` block, which runs once at class initialisation (see the previous chapter).

#### Static members are not polymorphic

You can write `someAccount.issued()`, and it compiles, but it is resolved from the *declared type* of the variable and never looks at the object. It is confusing, and linters flag it; always call statics through the class name. A subclass can declare a static method with the same signature, which *hides* rather than overrides the original (see the inheritance chapter).

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Static mutable state is global state. A `static int counter` incremented by many threads is a race condition, and static state makes tests depend on each other, because it survives from one test to the next. Use static for constants, pure helper functions and factory methods. For shared mutable data, pass an object in (dependency injection, which Spring does for you).

### Static nested classes: a preview

A class declared inside another class with the `static` modifier is a **static nested class**. It is an ordinary class that happens to live in the namespace of its outer class and can see the outer class's private static members. This book's examples use them (`Counter`, `Account` above) so that one file can hold several small classes. They do not hold a hidden reference to an outer object. The other kinds of nested class (inner, local, anonymous) are covered later in this Part.

### Access modifiers

Java has four access levels. They answer: from where in the program can this class, field, method or constructor be reached?

blocks.caption: Who can access a member? (✓ = allowed)

blocks.text: Top-level classes can only be `public` or package-private; the other two levels apply to members. The compiler enforces these rules. The following test class sits in the default package and extends a class from `com.example.lib`:

blocks.title: com/example/lib/Widget.java
Other.java

blocks.code:
$ javac -d out com/example/lib/Widget.java Other.java
Other.java:7: error: prot has protected access in Widget
        System.out.println(w.prot);   // protected via a Widget reference: error
                            ^
Other.java:8: error: pkg is not public in Widget; cannot be accessed from outside package
        System.out.println(pkg);      // package-private: error
                           ^
Other.java:9: error: priv has private access in Widget
        System.out.println(priv);     // private: error
                           ^
3 errors
blocks.title: Compile it

blocks.text:
What to notice. `protected` is the subtle one. A subclass in another package may use the member only on *its own* instances (`this.prot`, or an object of the subclass type), not on an arbitrary `Widget` reference, which is why `w.prot` fails while plain `prot` works. Within the same package, `protected` behaves like package-private plus the inheritance rule.

#### Choosing a level

Start with `private`. Widen only when a real caller needs it: package-private for helpers shared inside one package, `public` for the actual API, `protected` rarely (it publishes your internals to every subclass author forever). Every public member is a promise you must keep.

### Packages

A **package** is a named group of related classes, and it maps to a directory: class `com.example.lib.Widget` lives in `com/example/lib/Widget.java`. Packages do three jobs: they avoid name clashes (two libraries can both have a class `Date`), they define the package-private access boundary, and they organise code. By convention package names are all lower case and start with a reversed domain name you own (`com.example.shop`), which makes them globally unique.

A file starts with `package com.example.lib;`. To use a class from another package, import it (`import` `java.util.List;`) or write its full name. `import java.util.*;` imports every class in that package on demand but not sub-packages (`java.util.concurrent` needs its own import). Everything in `java.lang` (`String`, `Math`, `Object`) is imported automatically. A `static import` (`import static java.lang.Math.max;`) lets you call a static member without the class name; use it sparingly, mostly for constants and test assertions.

Using a package is a build concern too: `javac -d out ...` writes class files into a matching directory tree, and `java` `-cp out com.example.lib.Main` runs one. Part 1 covered the classpath; Part 11 covers modules, which add a stronger boundary above packages.

### Encapsulation

**Encapsulation** means a class hides how it stores its data and offers a small set of operations instead. The reward is freedom to change: the class `Temperature` can store Celsius today and Kelvin tomorrow, and no caller breaks, provided they only used the methods. The cost of not doing it is that every caller becomes coupled to every field.

#### Getters and setters: a fair debate

The textbook pattern is private fields with public `getX()` and `setX()`. Used mechanically it adds nothing: a class with a getter and setter for every field is just a struct with extra typing. The question to ask is "what operation does the caller want?". A `BankAccount` should offer `deposit(amount)` and `withdraw(amount)`, which can check rules, rather than `setBalance(...)`, which lets anyone put in any number. Guidelines:

- Expose a getter only when callers truly need to read the value; do not generate them by reflex.
- Prefer behaviour methods that enforce invariants over setters. If a setter must exist, validate in it.
- Prefer immutable objects (next section) and, for plain data carriers, records (covered later in this Part), which give you accessors with no boilerplate.
- Frameworks matter in practice: JavaBeans conventions (`getX`/`isX`/`setX`) are what Spring, Jackson and JPA use to read and write properties, so entity and DTO classes often keep them. That is a framework requirement, not a design ideal.

### Immutability and defensive copies

An **immutable** object never changes after construction. `String`, `Integer`, `BigDecimal` and `LocalDate` are immutable. Immutable objects are easy to reason about, safe to share between threads without locking, and safe as `HashMap` keys. The recipe for an immutable class:

1. Declare the class `final` (so no subclass can add mutable state).
2. Make all fields `private final`.
3. Provide no setters; "modifying" methods return a new object.
4. Make a **defensive copy** of any mutable object received in the constructor, and return copies (or unmodifiable views) from getters.

Step 4 is the one people miss. If the constructor stores the caller's list, the caller still holds a reference to it and can change it behind your back:

blocks.title: Defensive.java

blocks.code:
$ java Defensive.java
leaky: [Emma, Hacked]
safe: [Dune, Emma]
UnsupportedOperationException
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text: What to notice. `final` on `books` only froze the *reference*; the list behind it kept changing in `LeakyShelf`. `List.copyOf` (Java 10+) creates an unmodifiable snapshot, so changes to `src` do not reach `SafeShelf` and the getter can safely return it. For an array field, use `array.clone()` on the way in and out. For a mutable element type such as the legacy `java.util.Date`, copy each element too (`new Date(d.getTime())`), or better, avoid mutable types and use `java.time`.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: `final` means "this variable cannot be reassigned", not "this object cannot change". `final List<String> xs = new` `ArrayList<>(); xs.add("ok");` compiles and works. Immutability comes from the design of the class, not from the keyword on a field.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In Spring applications, immutable configuration and value objects are everywhere. Constructor injection (`final` fields set in the constructor) is preferred over field injection because the bean cannot be observed half-built and tests can create it with plain `new`. DTOs are increasingly records.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do you make a class immutable? Is `String` immutable because its field is `final`? `final` class, `private final` fields, no setters, defensive copies of mutable inputs and outputs. `String` is immutable because it exposes no operation that changes its internal state (its array is private and never leaked), not merely because a field is `final`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Use `static` for class-level constants, helpers and factories; avoid shared mutable static state.

- Four access levels: `private`, package-private, `protected`, `public`. Start private and widen only when needed.
- A package is a namespace, a directory and an access boundary; names are lower case, reversed-domain.
- Encapsulate behaviour, not just fields: offer operations that enforce invariants, not a setter per field.
- Immutability needs a final class, private final fields, no setters, and defensive copies in and out.
- `final` freezes a reference, not the object it refers to.

Suppose your library system has `Book`, `Magazine` and `DVD`. All three have a title and can be borrowed. Copying the same fields and methods into three classes is tedious and error-prone: fix a bug in one and the other two keep it. **Inheritance** lets a class reuse another class's members by declaring `extends`: the new class (the **subclass**, or child) automatically has everything the **superclass** (parent) has, and may add to it or change it. Inheritance also creates an *is-a* relationship that the type system understands, which is what makes polymorphism, the next chapter's subject, possible.

Inheritance is also the most over-used feature in object-oriented programming. This chapter teaches the mechanics precisely, and ends with when not to use it.

### extends and super

blocks.title: Hier.java

blocks.code:
$ java Hier.java
Vehicle(Mini)
Car(4)
Car Mini doors=4
Car Mini doors=4
true
vehicle car
Vehicle(truck)
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
What to notice. Each class extends exactly one other class: Java has single inheritance of classes (multiple inheritance of *type* is available through interfaces, covered later). Every class without an `extends` clause extends `java.lang.Object`, so every object has `toString`, `equals`, `hashCode` and friends. The superclass constructor runs first (`Vehicle(Mini)` printed before `Car(4)`), which is why a subclass constructor starts with `super(...)`. The keyword `super` has two uses: `super(args)` as the first statement of a constructor calls a superclass constructor, and `super.method()` calls the superclass's version of a method from inside an override. `Car.describe()` could have called `super.describe()` to reuse the parent's behaviour and then added to it.

#### Constructors in a hierarchy

Constructors are **not inherited**. If you write no `super(...)` call, the compiler inserts `super();` for you, and that fails to compile if the parent has no no-argument constructor:

blocks.title: Bad1.java

blocks.code:
$ javac Bad1.java
Bad1.java:6: error: constructor Parent in class Parent cannot be applied to given types;
        Child() { }              // implicit super() - Parent has no such constructor
                ^
  required: String
  found:    no arguments
  reason: actual and formal argument lists differ in length
blocks.title: Compile it

blocks.text:
The fix is an explicit `super("something")`. Since Java 25 (JEP 513, flexible constructor bodies) you may run statements *before* `super(...)` as long as they do not use `this`, for example validating an argument or computing a value to pass up. That is not runnable on Java 21, so earlier code resorts to static helper methods for the same job.

### Overriding rules

A subclass **overrides** an inherited instance method by declaring one with the same name and the same parameter types. The rules the compiler enforces are the Liskov Substitution Principle in code form: anything that works with the parent must still work with the child.

rows: Cannot be weaker than the parent's (a `public` method cannot become package-private); may be wider.
Same, or a subtype of the parent's (a **covariant return**: `Car describe()` overrides `Vehicle describe()`). Primitives must match exactly.
May throw fewer, or narrower, checked exceptions than the parent; never broader new ones. Unchecked exceptions are unrestricted.
Cannot be overridden; a same-signature static method **hides** the parent's.
Not inherited, so not overridable; the subclass method is unrelated.
blocks.caption: Overriding rules.

blocks.text: Here is one class that breaks four of those rules at once, together with what the compiler says (shortened):

blocks.text:
#### Always write @Override

`@Override` asks the compiler to verify that you really override something. Without it, a typo (`tostring()`) or a wrong parameter type silently creates a *new* method that is never called polymorphically. The next chapter shows exactly this bug with `equals(Point)` versus `equals(Object)`.

#### Hiding is not overriding

A `static` method with the same signature in a subclass, and a field with the same name, **hide** the parent's. Which one you get depends on the *declared type* of the expression, not on the object:

blocks.title: Hide.java

blocks.code:
$ java Hide.java
P C.id+P.id
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
The variable `p` is declared `P`, so `p.who()` is `P.who()`, even though the object is a `C`. The instance method `id()` was overridden, so the object's real class decided. Rule of thumb: only instance methods are polymorphic; fields and static methods are looked up using the declared type.

### final classes and methods

`final` on a method forbids overriding; on a class forbids extending (`String`, `Integer`, and all records are final). Use `final` when a class is not designed for extension, which is true of most classes. A class that allows subclassing must document how overridable methods are used by other methods (the "self-use" contract), otherwise a subclass author cannot know which override is safe. Joshua Bloch's advice in *Effective Java*, "design and document for inheritance or else prohibit it", is the standing guidance. Sealed classes (a later chapter in this Part) offer a middle path: a closed set of permitted subclasses.

### protected and the fragile base class

`protected` lets subclasses reach into a parent's fields and helper methods. It is convenient, and it welds the subclass to the parent's internals: if the parent later changes how it stores its data, every subclass that touched the field breaks. This is the **fragile base class problem**. A classic example, from *Effective Java*: a `CountingSet` that extends `HashSet` and overrides `add` and `addAll` to count insertions.

blocks.title: CS.java

blocks.code:
$ java CS.java
6
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
Three elements were added but the counter says 6: the inherited `addAll` implementation calls `add` for each element, so each element was counted twice. The subclass depended on an implementation detail of the parent, which the parent never promised and may change in any release.

The remedy is usually **composition**: instead of `class CountingSet extends HashSet`, write a class that has a `Set` field and forwards calls to it, adding the counting on top. The forwarding class depends only on the public contract of `Set`. A later chapter on class design develops this fully ("favour composition over inheritance").

### When to extend

Use inheritance when all of these are true: the relationship really is *is-a* in every context (a `Car` is a `Vehicle` everywhere a vehicle is accepted), the parent was designed for extension, and you want substitutability (callers should be able to use a child where a parent is expected). Do not use it just to reuse code: a `Stack` that extends `ArrayList` can be indexed and cleared from outside, and a `Square` that extends `Rectangle` breaks the promise that setting the width does not change the height. When in doubt, use composition or an interface.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Run `javac -Xlint:all` to get warnings for risky overriding patterns. It also flags missing `serialVersionUID`, raw types and many other problems at no cost. Many teams make warnings fail the build.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Can you override a static method? A private method? A constructor? No to all three. A static method with the same signature hides the parent's, resolved by declared type. A private method is not inherited, so a same-named method in the subclass is a different method. Constructors are not inherited and cannot be overridden; you call them via `super(...)`.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What happens if a superclass constructor calls an overridden method? The overridden version in the subclass runs while the subclass's fields are still at their default values, because the subclass initialisers have not run yet. Avoid calling overridable methods in constructors.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Single inheritance of classes with `extends`; every class ends at `Object`. Constructors are never inherited; `super(...)` chains them, superclass first.

- Overriding: same signature, access not weaker, covariant return, no broader checked exceptions, never `final` or `static`. Always write `@Override`.
- Fields and static methods are hidden, not overridden; the declared type decides which one you get.
- `protected` couples subclasses to parent internals (the fragile base class problem).
- Prefer composition; extend only for a true, designed-for-extension is-a relationship.

Polymorphism ("many forms") is the payoff of inheritance and interfaces: you write code against a general type, and each object responds in its own way. A method `printAll(List<Shape> shapes)` calls `shape.area()` and gets a circle's area for circles and a rectangle's for rectangles, without a single `if`. New shapes can be added later and `printAll` never changes. To use this safely you must know *which* decisions the compiler makes and which the JVM makes at run time. Mixing them up is the cause of a famous category of interview trick questions and of real bugs.

### Static type versus dynamic type

Every reference expression has two types. The **static type** (declared type) is what the source code says: in `Animal a =` `new Dog();` the static type of `a` is `Animal`. The **dynamic type** (runtime type) is the actual class of the object the reference points to: `Dog`. The compiler knows only static types. It uses them to decide what you are allowed to write: `a.bark()` is rejected if `Animal` has no `bark()`, even though the object could do it.

The JVM knows dynamic types. When a method is invoked on an object, the JVM picks the implementation by the object's real class. That is **dynamic dispatch**, also called late binding or runtime polymorphism.

### Overriding versus overloading

These two words sound alike and work in opposite ways.

blocks.text: The program below shows all the dispatch decisions in one place: field hiding, overriding, and an overload that looks like an override.

blocks.title: Dispatch.java

blocks.code:
$ java Dispatch.java
Woof
animal-field
dog-field
Dog meets Dog
Animal meets Animal
CCE: class Dispatch$Animal cannot be cast to class Dispatch$Dog (
pattern ok: Woof
false
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
What to notice, line by line:

- `a.sound()` prints `Woof`: the method is overridden, so the object's class (`Dog`) decides.
- `a.name` prints `animal-field`: **fields are never polymorphic**. A `Dog` object contains two separate `name` fields (one from `Animal`, one that hides it), and the static type picks which.
- `a.greet(d)` prints `Animal meets Animal`. `Dog.greet(Dog)` does not override `Animal.greet(Animal)`; it is an overload with a different parameter type. The compiler looked at `a`'s static type `Animal`, found only `greet(Animal)`, and generated a call to exactly that method. Adding `@Override` to `Dog.greet(Dog)` would have turned this into a compile error and saved you.
- The `ClassCastException` message names both classes. Casting down to a subtype is checked at run time.
- `null instanceof Animal` is `false`; `instanceof` never throws on `null`.

#### The classic equals bug

The same trap appears in real code. Here `equals(P)` overloads rather than overrides `Object.equals(Object)`:

blocks.title: Over.java

blocks.code:
$ java Over.java
true false
false
Object
String
long
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
`a.equals(b)` is true (the overload matches), but `a.equals(ob)` is false because the static type of `ob` is `Object`, which selects `Object.equals`, the inherited identity version. `HashSet.contains` calls `equals(Object)`, so the set does not find the "equal" point. With `@Override` on that method the compiler would have refused. The last three lines show overload resolution: it uses the static type (`show(o)` picks the `Object` version), and prefers widening (`int` to `long`) over boxing (`Integer`) over varargs. Phases are tried in that order: no boxing and no varargs first, then boxing, then varargs.

Conceptually each loaded class has a **method table** (a *vtable*): an array of pointers to the implementation of each virtual method. A subclass copies its parent's table and replaces the entries for methods it overrides; new methods are appended. Each object's header points to its class, so `a.sound()` becomes "load the class from the object, index into the table at the slot number assigned to `sound`, jump". The slot number is the same in every subclass, which is why the compiler can emit a fixed instruction while the target varies. Interface methods use a similar structure (an itable), searched by interface. This describes the idea; HotSpot's exact layout is an implementation detail.

You can see the compile-time part in bytecode. Take this small program:

Bytecode of run(), then the calls in Dispatch

blocks.text:
The instruction names `Call$A.hi`, the *static* type, and the JVM resolves it to `B.hi` when run with a `B`. The last two lines are the overload story: the compiler wrote the chosen parameter types (`Dog` or `Animal`) into the method descriptor. There was no `invokevirtual` for `Dog.greet(Animal)` because that method does not exist; overload choice is finished before the program runs.

The five invoke instructions tell you how each call is bound:

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Is dynamic dispatch slow? Less than you would expect. The JIT compiler (Part 1, Part 9) watches which classes actually reach a call site. If only one does (monomorphic), it inlines that method behind a cheap class check; with two, it inlines both (bimorphic). Only call sites that see many classes (megamorphic) pay for a real table lookup. Class hierarchy analysis lets it skip dispatch entirely when no loaded subclass overrides the method.

### Casting and instanceof

An **upcast** (treating a `Dog` as an `Animal`) is always safe and needs no syntax: `Animal a = new Dog();`. A **downcast** goes the other way, `Dog d = (Dog) a;`, and is checked by the JVM at run time: if the object is not a `Dog` (or a subclass), you get `ClassCastException`. The compiler also rejects casts between unrelated classes (`(String) new Dog()` does not compile), but allows any cast between related types and between a class and an interface, because the runtime object might satisfy it.

Before a downcast, test with `instanceof`. Since Java 16, pattern matching for `instanceof` tests and casts in one step:

Frequent downcasting is a smell. If you find a chain of `if (x instanceof A) ... else if (x instanceof B) ...` repeated in several places, the behaviour probably belongs in a method on the types themselves (polymorphism), or, for a closed set of types, in a `switch` over a sealed hierarchy with pattern matching, covered later in this Part. Note also that after generics erasure you cannot write `x instanceof List<String>`; only the raw type can be tested at run time.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Calling an overridable method on `this` from a constructor, a field read through the wrong type, an overload that is not an override, a static method called "through an object": all four are the same lesson. Only instance methods are late-bound; everything else is decided by static types or by the order of initialisation.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between method overloading and overriding? Which is compile-time and which is run-time polymorphism? Overloading: same name, different parameters, chosen at compile time by static argument types. Overriding: subclass replaces a parent's instance method with the same signature, chosen at run time by the receiver's actual class. Overriding is the true (run-time) polymorphism.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What does this print? `Animal a = new Dog(); System.out.println(a.name);` when both classes declare a field `name`. The `Animal` field, because fields are resolved by the static type. Only methods are dispatched dynamically.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Every expression has a static type (compiler) and a dynamic type (JVM). Instance methods dispatch on the dynamic type; fields, static methods and overload choice use the static type.

- Overloading is chosen at compile time; overriding at run time. Always use `@Override`.
- Dispatch is a method-table lookup in concept; the JIT removes most of the cost at monomorphic call sites.
- Upcasts are implicit and safe; downcasts are runtime-checked. Use `instanceof` patterns, but prefer polymorphic methods over type tests.

Inheritance lets a subclass reuse code. But often you want something different: to say "anything that can be drawn", "anything that can be compared", without saying how it is drawn or compared, and without forcing all such things into one family tree. Java gives you two tools for this. An **abstract class** is a partly finished class that cannot be instantiated. An **interface** is a pure contract, a list of capabilities that any class, anywhere in the hierarchy, can promise to provide. Knowing when to use which is a staple of design discussions and interviews.

### Abstract classes

An `abstract` class is declared with the keyword and may contain **abstract methods**: a signature with no body. A concrete subclass must implement every abstract method, or itself be declared abstract. You cannot call `new` on an abstract class; its purpose is to be extended.

Why would you want that? To share real code and state between related classes while forcing each to supply the part that differs (the **template method** idea). `Shape` below holds the colour and the drawing routine, but leaves `area()` to the subclasses:

blocks.title: Shapes.java

blocks.code:
$ java Shapes.java
red Circle area=7.07
Drawable:Circle
blue Rect area=6.00
Drawable:Rect
text hello
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
What to notice. `Shape` is abstract but has a constructor, a `private final` field and a concrete method: abstract classes are real classes with state. The loop is polymorphism in action: `s.draw()` runs `Shape.draw`, which calls `area()`, which is dispatched to the circle's or rectangle's version. An abstract class may have no abstract methods at all (just to block instantiation), and a class with even one abstract method must itself be declared abstract.

### Interfaces

An **interface** declares a set of methods that implementing classes must provide. A class says `implements Drawable` and may implement any number of interfaces. Members of an interface are implicitly `public`; fields are implicitly `public static final` constants. An interface has no constructors and no instance state.

Think of an interface as a role. `Comparable` means "can be ordered", `Runnable` means "can be run", `AutoCloseable` means "can be closed". A `String`, an `Integer` and your own `Book` class share nothing in the hierarchy yet all can be `Comparable`. Code written against the interface works with all of them, and tests can substitute simple fake implementations.

#### Default, static and private methods (Java 8 and 9)

Before Java 8 an interface could not change without breaking every implementor: adding a method broke all existing classes. **Default methods** (Java 8) have a body and are inherited unless a class overrides them, which let the library designers add `List.sort` and `Collection.stream` without breaking decades of existing code. **Static methods** in interfaces (Java 8) hold factories and helpers belonging to the contract (`Drawable.of(...)`, `List.of(...)`); they are not inherited by implementing classes and must be called through the interface name. **Private methods** (Java 9) let default methods share code without exposing it, as `name()` does in `Drawable`.

#### Multiple inheritance of behaviour: the diamond rules

Because a class may implement several interfaces that now carry default methods, two inherited defaults can collide. The compiler applies three rules, in this order:

1. **A class wins.** A method declared in the class or inherited from a superclass beats any interface default.
2. **The most specific interface wins.** If one interface extends the other and both define the default, the sub-interface's version is used.
3. **Otherwise the class must resolve it.** If two unrelated interfaces provide the same default, the class will not compile until it overrides the method, optionally choosing one with `Interface.super.method()`.

### Functional interfaces: a teaser

An interface with exactly one abstract method is a **functional interface**. A lambda expression or method reference can then stand in for an implementing class. `Drawable.of` above returned `() -> System.out.println(...)` for the same reason (`Drawable` has a single abstract method, `draw`).

7 12
9

`@FunctionalInterface` is optional but makes the compiler check the single-method rule. Part 7 covers lambdas, the standard interfaces in `java.util.function` and streams in depth.

### Marker interfaces

An interface with no methods at all is a **marker interface**; it just tags a class. `Serializable` says "this class may be converted to bytes", `Cloneable` changes how `Object.clone` behaves, `RandomAccess` tells algorithms that indexed access is fast. They are checked with `instanceof`. Annotations are the modern way to tag things, but the marker interface has one real advantage: it is a *type*, so a method can demand it in its signature.

### Abstract class or interface?

blocks.caption: Abstract class versus interface.

blocks.text: Practical guidance: **start with an interface** for the contract. Add an abstract class if several implementations genuinely share state or logic, and have it implement the interface. The JDK does this repeatedly: `List` (interface) with `AbstractList` (skeleton class) with `ArrayList` (concrete). Callers depend on `List`, never on `ArrayList`, which is how you can swap implementations later. Choose an abstract class when you need a constructor, protected hooks, or non-public state; choose an interface when unrelated classes may need to play the role, which is almost always the more flexible choice.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Spring and most backend code is written against interfaces. A `UserRepository` interface with a JPA implementation in production and an in-memory fake in tests; a `PaymentGateway` interface with one implementation per provider. The container wires the implementation in, and callers never name the concrete class. Spring Data even generates the implementation of your repository interface at start-up.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Name interfaces by role (`Comparable`, `Closeable`, `PaymentGateway`), not with an `I` prefix. Java style does not use `IPaymentGateway`. If an implementation has no better name, `Default...` or `...Impl` is common.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Can an interface have a constructor or instance variables? What happens when two interfaces provide the same default method? No constructor and no instance state; fields are `public static final`. If a class inherits two unrelated defaults with the same signature, it does not compile until it overrides the method (it can delegate with `A.super.m()`). A class method always wins over an interface default, and a more specific sub-interface wins over its parent.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Abstract class versus interface: which would you choose, and why? Interface by default, because a class can implement many and the contract stays free of implementation. Abstract class when implementations share state or code, needing constructors or protected helpers. Often both: interface plus an abstract skeleton.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
An abstract class is a partial class with state and constructors; an interface is a contract that unrelated classes can implement.

- Interfaces may carry `default`, `static` and `private` methods; they carry constants but no instance state.
- Diamond rules: class wins, then the most specific interface, otherwise you must override.
- A functional interface has one abstract method and can be implemented by a lambda.
- Design to the interface; add an abstract skeleton class only when implementations share code.

Every class in Java, whether you wrote `extends` or not, descends from `java.lang.Object`. It is the single root of the hierarchy, so a variable of type `Object` can hold any reference, and every object responds to a small set of methods: `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString`, `getClass`, `clone`, the wait/notify family and the legacy `finalize`. Collections, logging, debuggers and frameworks all rely on these. Overriding them correctly is among the most tested topics in Java interviews and among the most common sources of subtle bugs, so this chapter spends most of its time on `equals` and `hashCode`.

### toString

`toString()` returns a text representation of the object. The default implementation returns the class name, an `@`, and the hash code in hexadecimal, such as `java.lang.Object@659e0bfd` (typical output; the number varies between runs). It is useless to humans. `System.out.println(obj)`, string concatenation, loggers and debuggers all call `toString`, so a readable override is the cheapest debugging aid there is:

Include the fields that identify the object, never secrets (passwords, tokens, card numbers), because `toString` ends up in log files. Records and IDE generators produce this for you.

### getClass

`getClass()` returns the `Class` object describing the runtime class of an object; it is `final` and cannot be overridden. `obj.getClass() == Point.class` is true only for *exactly* that class, whereas `obj instanceof Point` is also true for subclasses. `getClass().getName()` gives `java.lang.String`, while `getSimpleName()` gives `String`; arrays have names like `[I` for `int[]`. The distinction between these two tests matters when you write `equals`, as the next section shows.

### equals and hashCode

#### What == means and what equals means

For references, `==` asks "are these the same object?" (identity). `equals` asks "do these represent the same value?" (equality). `Object.equals` is just `==`, so a class that wants value equality must override it. `String`, `Integer`, `List`, `LocalDate` and all records do.

#### The equals contract

The Javadoc requires `equals` to be an **equivalence relation**, and to be consistent:

- **Reflexive:** `x.equals(x)` is true.
- **Symmetric:** `x.equals(y)` is true exactly when `y.equals(x)` is.
- **Transitive:** if `x.equals(y)` and `y.equals(z)`, then `x.equals(z)`.
- **Consistent:** repeated calls give the same answer while nothing changed.
- **Non-null:** `x.equals(null)` is false, never an exception.

#### The hashCode contract

`hashCode()` returns an `int` used by hash-based collections (`HashMap`, `HashSet`) to choose a bucket. The rule that ties it to `equals`:

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.text: hashCode contract If `a.equals(b)` is true then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` must be true. The reverse need not hold (different objects may share a hash code, a collision), and the value must stay the same for the same object while the fields used by `equals` do not change.

Equal objects must produce equal hash codes, otherwise a hash collection looks in the wrong bucket and will not find an object that is "equal" to the one it holds.

#### Breaking the contract: a demonstration

This class overrides `equals` but forgets `hashCode`. A second class does both correctly, and a third shows what happens to a mutable key:

blocks.title: Equality.java

blocks.code:
$ java Equality.java
bad equals: true
bad contains equal point: false
good contains equal point: true
Point[3,4]
after mutation: null / null / size 1
blocks.title: Run it (the "bad contains" line is false in practice but depends on identity hash codes)

blocks.text:
What to notice.

- `BadPoint` objects are `equals`, but the default `hashCode` is derived from object identity, so `p1` and `p2` almost certainly land in different buckets, and `contains` answers false. The set silently misbehaves; no exception tells you.
- `Point` follows the recipe: the same fields feed both `equals` and `hashCode`. `Objects.hash(x, y)` is a convenient way to combine them (it allocates an array; for hot paths, compute `31 * x + y` by hand or use a record, which generates both for you).
- `MutableKey` shows the third rule. After `k.id = 2` the entry sits in the bucket for hash `1`, but a lookup with `k` now searches the bucket for hash `2`, and a lookup with a fresh key `1` finds the entry but `equals` fails against the mutated key. The entry is now unreachable yet still counted in `size`: a memory leak. **Never mutate a field that** **participates in** `hashCode` **while the object is a key or set member.** Prefer immutable keys.

#### equals: getClass or instanceof?

`Point.equals` above compared `getClass() != o.getClass()`, which means a `Point` never equals an instance of a subclass. Using `instanceof` instead lets a subclass instance equal a parent, but then symmetry breaks as soon as a subclass adds a field and its own `equals` considers it (the famous `ColorPoint` problem: `point.equals(colorPoint)` is true but the reverse is false). There is no way to extend an instantiable class, add a value component, and keep the `equals` contract. For a final class, `instanceof` is the clean choice, and for a non-final class, `getClass()` preserves the contract. Prefer composition for value types, or make the value class `final` or a record.

#### Recipe for equals and hashCode

1. Use the same fields in both methods, and only those fields.
2. In `equals`: check `this == o`, then null and class, then cast and compare. Compare primitives with `==` (`Double.compare` for `double`/`float`, to handle `NaN`), and objects with `Objects.equals(a, b)`, which is null-safe.
3. In `hashCode`: combine the same fields with `Objects.hash(...)` or the `31 * h + field` idiom.
4. Always pair them, always add `@Override` and always use the parameter type `Object`.
5. Better still, use a record (`record Point(int x, int y) {}`) or let the IDE generate it, and test it with a small unit test that puts equal objects into a `HashSet`.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: JPA entities are a famous trap. An entity whose `hashCode` uses a database-generated `id` changes hash code when it is first saved (null before, a number after), which breaks any `HashSet` that held it. Common guidance is to base `equals`/`hashCode` on a stable business key or return a constant `getClass().hashCode()`. Lombok's `@EqualsAndHashCode` has the same issue if applied naively to entities.

### clone, and why to avoid it

`Object.clone()` is `protected` and makes a shallow copy of an object: a new object whose fields hold the same values (the same *references*). It works only if the class implements the marker interface `Cloneable`, otherwise it throws `CloneNotSupportedException`. It creates objects without calling a constructor, interacts badly with `final` fields, and a subclass that forgets to override it correctly breaks the copy. Bloch's verdict in *Effective Java* is blunt: prefer a copy constructor or copy factory. The program shows the central problem, shared mutable state:

blocks.title: Cloning.java

blocks.code:
$ java Cloning.java
[99, 2, 3] shared=true
[1, 2, 3]
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
The "copy" `b` shares the array with `a`, so changing one changed the other. A correct `clone` must also clone the array (`copy.scores = scores.clone()`), which is why the copy constructor is simpler. Arrays are the one place where `clone()` is routine: `int[] copy = original.clone()` is fine and idiomatic (shallow for arrays of objects).

### finalize is on its way out

`Object.finalize()` was meant to release resources just before garbage collection. It is unpredictable (it may run late or never), slows collection, can resurrect objects and has security problems. It has been deprecated for removal since Java 18 (JEP 421), and the compiler now warns when you override it (`warning: [removal] finalize() in Object has` `been deprecated and marked for removal`). Release resources deterministically with `try`-with-resources and `AutoCloseable` (Part 5); use `java.lang.ref.Cleaner` for the rare native-handle safety net.

### wait, notify and the rest

`wait()`, `notify()` and `notifyAll()` are thread-coordination primitives on every object, tied to its monitor lock; Part 8 explains them. `hashCode()` for the default identity version is not the memory address, but a value generated by the JVM and stored in the object header the first time it is requested.

### compareTo and consistency with equals

`Comparable.compareTo` defines a natural ordering, used by `Collections.sort`, `TreeSet` and `TreeMap`. It is not part of `Object`, but it must be **consistent with equals**: `a.compareTo(b) == 0` should imply `a.equals(b)`. The JDK itself violates this in one well-known place, which makes a revealing demo:

blocks.title: Cmp.java

blocks.code:
$ java Cmp.java
false true
HashSet size 2, TreeSet size 1
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text: `BigDecimal.equals` considers scale (`1.0` is not `1.00`), `compareTo` does not. So a `HashSet` (uses `equals`) holds two elements while a `TreeSet` (uses `compareTo`) holds one. If you write your own `compareTo`, keep it consistent with `equals`, and if you cannot, document it as `BigDecimal` does. Never implement `compareTo` by subtracting integers (`return a -` `b`): overflow gives wrong signs; use `Integer.compare(a, b)`.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the contract between equals() and hashCode()? What happens if you override only one? Equal objects must have equal hash codes. If you override `equals` only, hash collections cannot find equal objects (they look in the wrong bucket); if only `hashCode`, `equals` still compares identity, so lookups find the right bucket but fail the equality check. Both must use the same fields, and keys must not change while stored.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why is `clone()` considered broken? What do you use instead? It is a shallow copy by default, bypasses constructors, needs a marker interface that has no methods, and clashes with `final` fields. Use a copy constructor, a copy factory (`List.copyOf`) or an immutable design; `array.clone()` is the accepted exception.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
All classes extend `Object`; override `toString` for readable logs, and never put secrets in it.

- `equals` must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent and null-safe; `hashCode` must agree with it (equal objects, equal hashes).
- Override both together, with the same fields, `@Override`, and the parameter type `Object`. Records do this for you.
- Do not mutate hash-relevant fields of objects used as keys; prefer immutable keys.
- Avoid `clone` (use copy constructors) and `finalize` (deprecated for removal); keep `compareTo` consistent with `equals`.

sections.title: Nested, Inner, Local and Anonymous Classes

blocks.text:
Most classes live in their own file at the top level. But sometimes a class exists only to serve one other class: a node inside a linked list, an iterator that walks one collection, a small callback used in exactly one place. Java lets you declare a class *inside* another class so that the helper stays next to the code that needs it, and so that it can reach private members it would otherwise have no access to. This chapter covers the four flavours, the hidden machinery that makes them work, and the one famous trap (the memory leak through the hidden outer reference).

### The four kinds at a glance

Everything declared inside another type is a **nested class**. There are four kinds, and the difference that matters most is whether an instance carries a hidden reference to an instance of the enclosing class.

Single-use implementation of an interface or abstract class
