blocks.text: The next listing shows a static nested class, an inner class and an anonymous class together, and prints the names the compiler gives them.

blocks.title: Counter.java

blocks.code:
$ java Counter.java
1 2 hits=2
true
prod
101
Counter$1
Counter$Ticket
Counter$Config
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `c.new Ticket()` is the syntax for creating an inner object: you must supply the outer instance. Inside `Counter`'s own instance methods you can write plain `new Ticket()` and `this` is used.
- `Ticket` updates the private field `hits` of `Counter` directly. Nested classes and their outer class share private access; that is a main reason to nest.
- `Counter.this` names the enclosing instance. If `Ticket` had its own `hits`, `hits` would mean the inner one and `Counter.this.hits` the outer one (shadowing).
- At runtime there is no nesting at all. The compiler produces separate class files named `Counter$Ticket`, `Counter$Config` and `Counter$1` (anonymous classes are numbered).

### Static nested versus inner: the hidden reference

Compile `Counter.java` with `javac` and inspect the inner class with `javap -p`. The compiler has added a field and a constructor parameter that you never wrote.

blocks.title: Inside an inner class

blocks.text: `this$0` is the hidden reference to the outer object, and the constructor takes the outer instance as its first parameter. A static nested class gets neither. This is why a static nested class is the right default: it costs nothing extra and cannot accidentally keep an outer object alive. **Make a nested class** `static` **unless it genuinely needs the outer** **instance.** IDEs will even suggest it.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Since JDK 18 the compiler leaves `this$0` out of an inner class when the class never uses the outer instance (JDK-8271623). So on a modern JDK the field exists only if the inner or anonymous class actually touches the outer object, or if the class is serializable. The leak below therefore depends on how you write the class, which is exactly what makes it hard to notice.

### Local classes and capturing variables

A **local class** is declared inside a method, constructor or block. It is visible only there. It can read local variables and parameters of the enclosing method, but only if they are **final or effectively final**: assigned once and never changed. Since Java 16 a local class can also be a record, an enum or an interface (all implicitly static, so they cannot capture locals).

blocks.title: Local.java

blocks.code:
$ java Local.java
hello 0
hello 1
hello 2
20
7 Local$1Local1
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text: **Why must captured variables be effectively final?** A local variable lives on the method's stack frame and dies when the method returns, but the object of the local or anonymous class may live much longer. So the compiler does not share the variable; it **copies the value** into a synthetic field of the new object. If the original could change afterwards, the copy would silently disagree with it, and if the copy could change, the method would not see it. Java resolves the confusion by forbidding both: the value is fixed, so copying is invisible. (Languages such as JavaScript capture the variable itself, which is a different and more confusing model.) The loop above copies `i` into `n` for exactly this reason: `i` changes on every iteration, so it cannot be captured.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Capturing a mutable *object* is fine; only the variable's reference must not change. `final List<String> log = new` `ArrayList<>();` can be captured and `log.add(...)` still works. The effectively-final rule protects the variable, not the object it points to. A common workaround, a one-element array `int[] count = {0};`, compiles but is shared mutable state: do not use it with threads, and prefer an `AtomicInteger` or restructure the code.

### Anonymous classes

An **anonymous class** declares and instantiates a class in one expression. It has no name, so it is used once, typically to implement an interface or extend a class with a small override:

Restrictions: no constructor (it has no name; arguments in `new Base(args) { ... }` go to the superclass constructor), it can extend a class **or** implement one interface, not both, and it can declare extra fields and methods but the outside world can call them only through `var`:

blocks.code:
var o = new Object() { int x = 5; int twice() { return x * 2; } };
System.out.println(o.twice());       // works: var keeps the anonymous type

blocks.text:
#### Anonymous class or lambda?

Since Java 8, a lambda replaces an anonymous class when the type is a **functional interface** (one abstract method). Lambdas are shorter and, as the next section shows, do not carry a hidden outer reference unless they use `this` or an outer member. They are not identical:

rows: Can have fields and several methods
its members can shadow outer variables
cannot redeclare an enclosing local name
blocks.caption: Anonymous class versus lambda.

blocks.text:
Use an anonymous class when you need more than one method, state, or a superclass that is not an interface. Otherwise use a lambda. The mechanism behind lambdas is explained in the chapter on lambdas in the functional Java Part.

### The memory leak through the hidden outer reference

An inner or anonymous class created in an instance method may hold `this$0`, which keeps the **entire outer object** reachable for as long as the inner object lives. If the outer object is big and the inner object is long-lived (queued task, registered listener, cached callback), you have a leak. The program below creates tasks that each belong to a `Report` holding a 10 MB array, and keeps only the tasks.

blocks.title: Leak.java

blocks.code:
$ java -Xmx100m Leak.java
Leak$Report$1 has field this$0
Leak$Report$2 has no fields
kept 1
kept 2
...
kept 8
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
        at Leak$Report.<init>(Leak.java:6)
        at Leak.main(Leak.java:31)
blocks.title: Run with a small heap (output trimmed)

blocks.text:
The first anonymous class uses `big`, so the compiler keeps `this$0` and each task pins 10 MB; the heap is exhausted after eight. The second one does not use the outer object, so on JDK 18 and later it carries nothing (on JDK 17 and earlier it would have carried `this$0` anyway). The same trap exists for inner `Iterator`s, listeners, and for the older Android and Swing idioms.

#### How to avoid it

- Default to `static` nested classes and pass in only what the helper needs.
- Prefer a lambda that uses no instance member, or a static factory method that returns the lambda.
- Do not store inner-class instances (listeners, callbacks) in static fields or long-lived collections without a way to remove them.
- When you suspect it, take a heap dump and look for `this$0` in the path to GC roots; the diagnostics Part shows how.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between a static nested class and an inner class? A static nested class is just a class that lives in another class's namespace; you create it with `new Outer.Nested()` and it has no outer instance. An inner class is non-static, needs an enclosing instance (`outer.new Inner()`), can use `Outer.this` and the outer's private members, and (when it uses them) holds a hidden `this$0` reference that can cause leaks. Prefer static nested unless you need the outer instance.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In frameworks you meet nested classes constantly: `Map.Entry` is a nested interface, `ArrayList` has a private inner `Itr` iterator, and Spring or Lombok builders are static nested `Builder` classes. Anonymous classes used to be the way to write callbacks (`new Callback() { ... }`); in modern code they are replaced by lambdas except when state or a superclass is needed.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Nest a class to keep a helper next to its only user and to share private access. Default to `static` nested.
- An inner class holds a hidden outer reference (`this$0`); the compiler passes it as an extra constructor argument.
- Local and anonymous classes capture local variables by copying their value, so those variables must be effectively final.
- Anonymous classes are numbered class files (`Outer$1`); use a lambda instead when the target is a functional interface.
- An inner object that outlives its outer object and uses it keeps the whole outer graph alive: a classic leak.

Many values come from a small, fixed set: days of the week, order states, card suits, HTTP methods. Before Java 5 programmers used `static final int` constants (`int PENDING = 0; int SHIPPED = 1;`), which have no type safety (you can pass `42`), no readable printing, and no namespace. A Java `enum` solves this: it is a class with a fixed, closed set of instances, each one a named constant. The compiler checks the type, you can print the name, and the constants can carry data and behaviour.

### Constants are objects

The simplest enum lists its constants. Each constant is a `public static final` instance of the enum class, created once when the class is initialised, so you may compare constants with `==`.
Every enum implicitly extends `java.lang.Enum<E>`, which supplies these methods:

rows: A fresh array of all constants in declaration order (added by the compiler).
Constant with that exact name; throws `IllegalArgumentException` if none (case-sensitive).
The constant's identifier as written. `final`; use it for stable storage.
Zero-based position in the declaration. Fragile: reordering changes it.
Compares ordinals, so constants sort in declaration order.
The enum type, even for constants with bodies.
blocks.caption: Methods every enum has.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Do not persist `ordinal()` (in a database column or a file). Inserting a new constant in the middle silently changes the meaning of every stored number. Store `name()` or an explicit code field instead. In JPA/Hibernate prefer `@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)`, not the default `ORDINAL`.

### Fields, constructors and methods

An enum can have fields, a constructor and methods. The constructor is implicitly `private`; it runs once per constant, with the arguments you write after the constant name.

blocks.title: Planets.java

blocks.code:
$ java Planets.java
[LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH]
10
2 HIGH
true
ADD + 13 class Planets$Op$1 class Planets$Op
MUL * 42 class Planets$Op$2 class Planets$Op
No enum constant Planets.Level.high
true
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `Op` declares an **abstract method** and gives each constant its own body. Each such constant is an anonymous subclass (`Planets$Op$1`), which is why `getClass()` differs from `getDeclaringClass()`. This is the strategy pattern with a fixed set of strategies and no `if` chains.
- A field of an enum should be `final`. A mutable field turns the constants into shared global state.
- The enum cannot be extended (`Level` is `final`; constants with bodies make it implicitly sealed), and it cannot be instantiated with `new`.

#### What the compiler generates

`javap -p` on `Planets$Level` shows the machinery: a `final` class extending `Enum`, one `public static final` field per constant, a private `$VALUES` array, and a static initializer that creates the constants.

blocks.title: Inspecting the compiled enum

blocks.text: `values()` returns a **copy** of `$VALUES` each call (to protect the original), so in a hot loop call it once and keep the array, or use `EnumSet.allOf`. Enums can also implement interfaces, which is how you give a family of constants a common type without inheritance:

blocks.title: Cmd.java

blocks.code:
$ java Cmd.java
150
-1
class java.lang.Enum
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The static lookup map is a standard idiom for parsing input. Note that it must be a `static` field declared after the constants, because the constants are created first.

### Enums in switch

An enum is the ideal `switch` selector. In a switch **expression** the compiler requires every constant to be covered (or a `default`), so adding a new constant later produces a compile error at every switch that forgot it. That is a real advantage over integer codes. With a classic switch **statement** over an enum, missing constants are silently ignored unless you add a `default` that throws.
Inside a `case` label you write the bare constant name (`RED`), not `Light.RED`. (Since Java 21, pattern-switch also lets you qualify enum constants in case labels when mixing types.)

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Avoid writing a `default` branch in a switch expression over an enum you own. The missing default is what lets the compiler tell you about new constants. Add `default` only for enums you do not control.

### EnumSet and EnumMap

Because an enum has a small known number of constants, specialised collections exist and are much faster than `HashSet` and `HashMap` for them.

- `EnumSet<E>` stores membership as bits (one `long` for up to 64 constants). Operations are a few machine instructions. Factories: `of`, `noneOf`, `allOf`, `range`, `complementOf`, `copyOf`.
- `EnumMap<K, V>` stores values in an array indexed by `ordinal()`. Iteration is in declaration order.

blocks.title: Sets.java

blocks.code:
$ java Sets.java
[SAT, SUN] [MON, TUE, WED, THU, FRI]
[TUE, WED, THU]
{MON=8, FRI=6}
RED GREEN YELLOW RED
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Note that `EnumMap` printed `MON` before `FRI` although `FRI` was inserted first. `EnumMap` needs the `Class` object (`Day.class`) in its constructor because the map cannot infer the key type at runtime (generics are erased). Use an `EnumSet` instead of an `int` bit-flag field (`READ | WRITE`) whenever you need a set of options.

### Singleton via enum

Joshua Bloch's recommendation in *Effective Java* is that a single-element enum is the best way to implement a singleton: the JVM guarantees the constant is created exactly once (class initialisation is thread-safe), and unlike a class with a private constructor, an enum cannot be duplicated by serialization or by reflection (`Constructor.newInstance` refuses to create enum instances).

blocks.title: Registry.java

blocks.code:
$ java Registry.java
1
2
true
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text: The limits: an enum singleton cannot extend another class (it already extends `Enum`), it is created eagerly at first use of the class, and in a Spring application you normally let the container manage singletons instead. The design patterns Part compares the other singleton forms.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Enum constants are created in a `static` initializer in declaration order. A constructor or constant body that touches a `static` field of the same enum (other than a compile-time constant) sees its default value, because the field is not yet initialised. The compiler reports a direct reference as an error.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why can you compare enums with `==`, and why is a single-element enum a good singleton? Each constant is created once per class loader and the type has no public constructor, so reference equality equals logical equality (and `==` is null-safe and type-checked at compile time). A single-element enum is a good singleton because class initialisation is atomic and thread-safe, serialization of enums preserves identity (it writes the name and uses `valueOf`), and reflection cannot create a second instance.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In backend code enums model statuses and types (`OrderStatus`, `PaymentMethod`) and often appear in JSON and database mappings. Jackson serialises an enum by `name()` by default; JPA by ordinal unless told otherwise (see the warning above). Keep an explicit `code` field when external systems need stable values and look it up through a static map.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- An enum is a class with a closed set of singleton instances; compare constants with `==`.
- Constants can have fields, constructors, methods and per-constant bodies (an abstract method per constant replaces `if` chains).
- Never persist `ordinal()`; store `name()` or an explicit code.
- Switch expressions over enums are checked for completeness, so omit `default` for your own enums.
- Use `EnumSet` and `EnumMap` for enum-keyed collections; a single-element enum is a safe singleton.

A huge amount of Java code is "data carriers": a class with a few fields, a constructor, getters, `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`. Writing a `Point` with two ints takes about thirty lines, and every line is a chance for a bug (forgetting a field in `equals`, for example). A **record** (Java 16) states the intent in one line and the compiler writes the rest:

blocks.code: record Point(int x, int y) {}

blocks.text:
That declares a final class with two private final fields, a constructor, accessors `x()` and `y()`, and `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` based on both components. A record is a *transparent, shallowly immutable carrier of values*: what you see in the header is its whole state and its public shape.

### What you get for free

blocks.title: Records.java

blocks.code:
$ java Records.java
Point[x=3, y=4] 3 true true
Money[cents=750, currency=EUR]
negative: -1
[Ana, Raj, Zed] [Ana, Raj]
UOE
true class java.lang.Record
x:int
y:int
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- The accessor is `x()`, not `getX()`. The generated `toString` is `Point[x=3, y=4]`.
- `Money` has a **compact constructor**: no parameter list, no field assignments. The body runs first and may validate or reassign the *parameters* (`currency = currency.toUpperCase()`); the compiler then assigns the fields from the parameters at the end. You cannot write `this.currency = ...` there.
- `Leaky` stores the caller's list: when `src` changes, the "immutable" record changes too. `Course` copies in its constructor, so it is safe.

### Constructors in depth

A record has one **canonical constructor** whose parameters match the components in order. You have three ways to deal with it:

1. Write nothing: the compiler generates it.
2. Write a **compact** constructor (as above) for validation and normalisation. The most common choice.
3. Write the full **explicit canonical** constructor with a parameter list and `this.x = x;` assignments. It must be at least as accessible as the record itself.

You can also add other constructors, but each one must start with `this(...)`, delegating eventually to the canonical one, so every instance passes through the same validation.

blocks.title: Rec2.java

blocks.code:
$ java Rec2.java
Range[lo=5, hi=5] 7 Range[lo=0, hi=0]
Line[from=Pair[first=0, second=0], to=Pair[first=3, second=4]]
Person[name=Ana, age=30]
v1.2 x|Named[name=  x ]
true
false
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- Records can be generic (`Pair<A, B>`), nested inside each other (`Line`), implement interfaces (`Comparable`, `Serializable`), and have static fields, static methods and ordinary instance methods.
- Records **cannot** declare instance fields beyond the components, cannot extend another class (they already extend `java.lang.Record`), and are implicitly `final`, so they cannot be extended.
- You may override an accessor (`Named.name()`), but the generated `toString`, `equals` and `hashCode` read the **fields**, not the accessors: the last line of output still shows `x` untrimmed. Keep accessors and fields consistent.
- Equality of components: reference components use `equals` (null-safe, so `null` works), primitives are compared by value, and `double`/`float` components compare with `Double.compare`, so `0.0` is not equal to `-0.0`.

### How it works under the hood

`javap -p` on a record shows what the compiler added. The three object methods are `final` and are implemented with `invokedynamic`, delegating to `java.lang.runtime.ObjectMethods` at link time instead of bytecode generated per record.

blocks.title: Inspecting a record

blocks.text:
The class file also stores a `Record` attribute listing the components, which is what `getRecordComponents()` reads (the last lines of the first program's output). Frameworks use it for reflection-based construction. `Jackson` (since 2.12), `Gson`, JPA projections and Spring MVC can all bind to records.

### Immutability, honestly

Fields are `final` and there are no setters, so you cannot reassign a component. But the immutability is **shallow**: if a component is a mutable object (an array, an `ArrayList`, a `Date`) the record's content can still change, as `Leaky` showed. To get real immutability:

- Copy mutable inputs in the compact constructor (`List.copyOf`, `Map.copyOf`, `array.clone()`), and
- Return unmodifiable views or copies from accessors if the component is an array, because the default accessor returns the very same array.

Records do not make *wither* operations (change one field, get a new object) automatic. You write them by hand: `Point` `withX(int nx) { return new Point(nx, y); }`. If a record has many components, a nested builder is still sensible.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: A record with an array component has identity-based `equals` for that component, because arrays do not override `equals`. `new R(new int[]{1}).equals(new R(new int[]{1}))` is `false`. Prefer a `List` and copy it, or override `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` yourself.

### When to use a record

Records fit values defined entirely by their data: coordinates, money amounts, DTOs (data transfer objects) returned by a REST controller, keys of a `HashMap` (the generated `hashCode` is correct), tuple-like return values from a method, and the variants of a sealed hierarchy (the next chapter). Local records (declared inside a method) are good for intermediate results in a stream pipeline.

They are the wrong tool when the object has identity or changing state (a bank account, a connection), when you need to hide the representation (a record's header is its public API; changing a component changes the API), or when it must be a JPA `@Entity` (entities need a no-arg constructor, mutable fields and proxies; records do not allow that).

#### Serialization notes

A record can implement `Serializable`, as `Person` did above (output proved the round trip). Records are serialized by their components only and **deserialized by calling the canonical constructor**, so your validation also runs on untrusted input; a plain class bypasses its constructor during deserialization, which is a classic security hole. `readObject`, `writeObject` and `serialPersistentFields` are ignored for records; only `writeReplace` and `readResolve` work. The default `serialVersionUID` of a record is `0L` unless you declare one. In practice most services serialize records as JSON rather than with Java serialization.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Are records immutable? What can you not do with them? Records are shallowly immutable: components are `final`, no setters exist, and the class is `final`. A mutable component can still be changed through its own methods, so you copy mutable inputs in the compact constructor. You cannot add instance fields, extend a class, or make the record abstract; it can implement interfaces and have static members and extra methods.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In Spring Boot, request and response bodies are very often records (`record CreateOrderRequest(String sku, int` `qty) {}`), with Bean Validation annotations (`@NotBlank`, `@Min`) placed on the components. Configuration properties can also be bound to records through constructor binding.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A record declares a transparent, final data carrier; the compiler generates fields, canonical constructor, accessors, `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString`.
- Validate and normalise in the compact constructor; every other constructor must delegate to the canonical one.
- Immutability is shallow: copy mutable components, especially collections and arrays.
- Records cannot extend classes or add instance fields, but can implement interfaces, be generic, nested and local.
- Use them for DTOs, keys, value objects and sealed-hierarchy variants, not for entities or objects with identity.

Normally anyone can extend a public class or implement a public interface. That openness is usually good, but sometimes you want the opposite: a type with a **closed, known set of subtypes**. A payment is either a card payment, a bank transfer or a wallet payment, and nothing else. An expression tree has exactly four node kinds. Before Java 17 you could only approximate this with a package-private constructor or an enum. A **sealed** class or interface (finalised in Java 17, JEP 409) lists exactly which classes may extend it, and the compiler enforces and exploits that list.

### Declaring a sealed hierarchy

blocks.title: Shapes.java

blocks.code:
$ java Shapes.java
Circle[r=1.0] -> 3.14
Rect[w=2.0, h=3.0] -> 6.00
Tri[b=4.0, h=5.0] -> 10.00
true
Circle
Rect
Tri
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### The rules

- `sealed` plus a `permits` list names the allowed direct subtypes. If all of them are in the **same source file**, `permits` may be omitted and the compiler infers them.
- Permitted subtypes must be in the same module (or, in the unnamed module, the same package) as the sealed type.
- Every permitted subtype must say what happens next, by choosing exactly one modifier: `final` (no more subclasses; records and enums are implicitly final), `sealed` (continues the closed hierarchy with its own `permits`) or `non-sealed` (reopens the hierarchy: anyone may extend it).
- The sealed type itself may be `abstract`, an interface or an ordinary class.

blocks.title: Sealed2.java

blocks.code:
$ java Sealed2.java
ok 7, error boom
true
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`Result<T>` shows the compact style: the variants are nested records inside the sealed interface, so no `permits` clause is needed. This `Ok`/`Err` shape is the same idea as `Result` types in Rust or Kotlin.

### What the compiler does for you

Two things make sealed types worth using. First, a class outside the list cannot extend the type:

blocks.code:
$ javac Bad.java
Bad.java:5: error: class is not allowed to extend sealed class: S (as it is not ...)
    record C() implements S {}
    ^
1 error
blocks.title: Adding a subtype that is not permitted (message shortened)

blocks.text: Second, a `switch` over a sealed type is checked for **exhaustiveness**: if you leave out a variant and have no `default`, it does not compile.

blocks.code:
$ javac Bad2.java
Bad2.java:5: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values
    static int f(S s) { return switch (s) { case A a -> 1; }; }
                               ^
1 error
blocks.title: Forgetting a variant

blocks.text: This reverses the usual cost of extension. With a normal interface it is cheap to add a new type and expensive to add a new operation (every implementer must change). With a sealed hierarchy plus `switch`, adding an *operation* is cheap (write one more method with a switch) and adding a *variant* is checked: every switch without a `default` breaks at compile time, pointing at exactly the code to update. That is the right trade for stable data models such as ASTs, events and results.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Do not add `default` to a switch over your own sealed type. The `default` silences the exhaustiveness check, which is the main benefit. If you need a catch-all for the future, make the hierarchy non-sealed or accept the compile error as a feature.

### Algebraic data types in plain Java

Computer scientists call this pattern an **algebraic data type**: a *sum type* (a value is exactly one of several variants, here the sealed interface) whose variants are *product types* (each bundles several values, here records). Sealed interfaces plus records give Java both halves. Combined with pattern matching (the next chapter) you can take a value apart in the `switch` itself:

blocks.title: Calc.java

blocks.code:
$ java Calc.java
(2 + 3 * -4) = -10
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The same job in classic object-oriented style would put an `eval()` method in every class (the visitor pattern if operations should live outside). Sealed types plus switch replace the visitor with ordinary code: no `accept` methods and no double dispatch. The design patterns Part returns to this.

#### Sealed versus enum versus open interface

Use an **enum** when the variants are fixed singletons with the same shape. Use a **sealed interface of records** when variants differ in what data they carry. Use a plain **interface** when third parties must be able to add implementations (plug-ins, `List`, `Comparable`).

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Sealed does not mean secret. Adding a permitted subtype is a source-incompatible change for everyone who switches over the type, even in other projects, so do not seal types in a public library API unless you are ready to treat new variants as breaking. The JDK itself seals very few types.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What problem do sealed classes solve, and how do they relate to `switch`? They let the author restrict which classes may extend a type, via `permits` (each subtype must be `final`, `sealed` or `non-sealed`). Because the compiler then knows the complete set of subtypes, a `switch` over the sealed type can be checked for exhaustiveness without a `default`, so adding a new variant produces compile errors where the code needs updating.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- `sealed ... permits` closes a hierarchy; each permitted subtype must be `final`, `sealed` or `non-sealed`.
- A switch over a sealed type is exhaustive without `default`, so new variants cause compile errors where handling is missing.
- Sealed interfaces plus records give algebraic data types (sum of products) in plain Java.
- Choose enums for same-shaped constants, sealed records for variants with different data, open interfaces for extension by others.
- Sealing a public API makes adding a variant a breaking change.

Code constantly asks "what kind of thing is this, and if it is that kind, give me its parts". Older Java answered with a test, a cast and a variable: three steps, one of which (the cast) the compiler cannot verify against the test. **Pattern** **matching** merges them: a *pattern* both tests a value and, on success, declares variables bound to its parts. Java has delivered it in stages: `instanceof` patterns (Java 16), `switch` patterns (Java 21), and record patterns (Java 21), with unnamed patterns (`_`) finalised in Java 22.

blocks.text: ### Type patterns with instanceof
The binding `s` is in scope exactly where the compiler can prove the match succeeded. That includes the right side of `&&`, and the code after a negated test that exits:

Because `||` could be reached on a failed match, `o instanceof String s || s.isEmpty()` does not compile. A pattern variable is not `final` automatically but it behaves like a local: you may reassign it unless declared `final`, though you rarely should.

### Pattern matching for switch

A `switch` (statement or expression, since Java 21) may switch on **any reference type** and use patterns as case labels. Cases are tried top to bottom; the first one that matches runs.

blocks.title: Patterns.java

blocks.code:
$ java Patterns.java
string of 5 | other
long string hello | not an int: hi | int 42
null!
int 7
big int 500
empty string
string abc
vertical line
line Point[x=0, y=0]->Point[x=2, y=3]
int array of 3
list size 2
something else: Double
6

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `case null` handles null explicitly. Without it, switching on `null` still throws `NullPointerException`, as with the old switch. You can combine: `case null, default -> ...`.
- `when` adds a **guard**: a boolean condition on the same case. `case Integer i when i > 100` must come before the plain `case Integer i`.
- `case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(int x2, int y2))` is a **record pattern with nested patterns**: it tests for `Line`, calls its accessors, tests the components for `Point`, and binds the ints, all in one line. `var` lets the compiler infer each component type.
- The last line shows a record pattern in `instanceof`.

### Record patterns

A **record pattern** `R(P1, P2, ...)` matches a record `R` and then matches each component against its sub-pattern. Nesting is unlimited, which is how you pull apart a tree in one expression (`case Add(Mul(Num(var a), Num(var b)),` `var rest)` in the expression example of the previous chapter). Under the hood the compiler calls the component accessors; if one throws, the exception is wrapped in a `MatchException`. A sub-pattern whose type is the same as (or wider than) the component type is called *total* and matches everything including `null`:

blocks.title: Nul.java

blocks.code:
$ java Nul.java
true
false
false
NPE
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The lines correspond to: `new Box(null) instanceof Box(Object c)` is `true` (a total pattern accepts the null component); `... instanceof Box(String c)` is `false` (a type test never matches null); `null instanceof Object x` is `false` (instanceof never matches null); and `switch (n) { case String s ...; default ... }` with `n == null` throws `NullPointerException` because there is no `case null`.

### Dominance and exhaustiveness

The compiler checks the order of your labels. A case that can never be reached because an earlier one already matches everything it would is **dominated**, and that is a compile error:

blocks.code:
$ javac Dom.java
Dom.java:5: error: this case label is dominated by a preceding case label
            case String s -> "s";
                 ^
1 error
blocks.title: A dominated label

blocks.text:
(`CharSequence` came first, and every `String` is a `CharSequence`.) The rules to remember:

- A more specific type must come **before** a more general one; guarded cases before unguarded ones of the same type.
- `default` (or `case null, default`) should be last. `case null` may be anywhere but is conventionally first.
- A switch expression, or a pattern switch statement, must be **exhaustive**: every possible value must be covered. For an `Object` selector that means a `default` or a total pattern like `case Object o`. For a sealed type, covering every permitted subtype is enough.

The compiler also checks sealed-record exhaustiveness through nested record patterns, which is what let the `show` method in the previous chapter work without `default`.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Fall-through and patterns do not mix: you cannot fall into a case that declares a pattern variable, because the variable might not be bound. Use arrow (`->`) cases, which never fall through. With colon cases a pattern label must end in `break`, `return` or similar before the next label.
