rows: Both in this chapter; guards use `when`.
`case Box(_)`, `catch (Exception _)`. Needs 22 or later, so not run here.
`case int i` on a `long` or `Object` selector. Not final; do not rely on it.
blocks.caption: Pattern-related features by version.

blocks.text: With unnamed patterns (Java 22 and later) you write `case Line(Point(var x, _), _)` to say "I do not care about this component", which removes unused variable names. They are not runnable on this book's JDK 21 and are shown only as a note. Primitive patterns are a preview feature in Java 25 (and still preview in 26 and 27 according to the JEP list), so treat them as experimental.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What does pattern matching for `instanceof`/`switch` give you over casts, and how does `switch` treat `null`? It combines the type test, the cast and the variable binding, so a wrong cast is impossible. A `switch` with patterns can have guards (`when`), nested record patterns and compile-time exhaustiveness checks. `null` selectors throw `NullPointerException` unless the switch has a `case null` label (possibly `case null, default`).

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Pattern switches over sealed event or command hierarchies are replacing long `if (x instanceof A) ... else if (x` `instanceof B)` chains in message handlers, parsers and compilers. They also replace many visitor-pattern implementations. In Spring services the typical use is mapping a sealed `Result` or domain event into an HTTP response.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A pattern tests a value and binds variables in one step: `o instanceof String s`, `case Circle c`, `case Point(var` `x, var y)`.
- Cases run top to bottom; more specific labels must precede general ones (dominance), and `when` adds a guard.
- Switch over any reference type; null needs `case null`, otherwise it throws NPE.
- Record patterns nest, and switches over sealed types are checked for exhaustiveness.
- `_` is final since Java 22; primitive patterns are still preview in 25, 26 and 27.

Java has two worlds of values. The eight **primitives** (`int`, `long`, `double`, `boolean`, ...) are raw numbers stored directly in variables and arrays; they are fast, cannot be `null`, and have no methods. **Objects** live on the heap and are reached through references. Many parts of the language only work with objects: generics (`List<int>` is illegal), collections, `Optional`, reflection, and anything typed `Object`. To bridge the two worlds, every primitive has a matching **wrapper** **class**, and the compiler converts between them automatically. That convenience hides several traps: `==` that works for 127 but not for 128, a `NullPointerException` on a line that contains no dot, and loops that quietly allocate millions of objects. This chapter shows how the conversion works so you can predict all of it.

### The eight wrappers

blocks.caption: Primitive types and their wrapper classes (all in java.lang).

blocks.text:
Wrapper objects are **immutable**: an `Integer` never changes its value, just like a `String`. They are also `final`, so you cannot subclass them. Each wrapper gives you three kinds of members: constants (`Integer.MAX_VALUE`, `Integer.BYTES`), static utilities that work on the primitive (`Integer.parseInt`, `Integer.compare`, `Integer.toBinaryString`, `Character.isDigit`), and instance methods that unwrap the value (`intValue()`, `doubleValue()`). The utilities are the main reason to know the classes even if you never box anything.

### Autoboxing and unboxing

**Boxing** converts a primitive to its wrapper; **unboxing** is the reverse. Since Java 5 the compiler inserts both for you. Nothing magical happens at run time: the compiler rewrites your code into calls to `valueOf` and `xxxValue`. The bytecode of `static int f(Integer i) { Integer j = i + 1; return j; }` shows it (trimmed `javap -c -p` output):

blocks.code:
$ javap -c -p Jp
  static int f(java.lang.Integer);
       0: aload_0
       1: invokevirtual #7    // Method java/lang/Integer.intValue:()I
       4: iconst_1
       5: iadd
       6: invokestatic  #13   // Method java/lang/Integer.valueOf:(I)Ljava/lang/Integer;
       9: astore_1
      10: aload_1
      11: invokevirtual #7    // Method java/lang/Integer.intValue:()I
      14: ireturn
blocks.title: Boxing is just method calls

blocks.text:
So `i + 1` unboxes `i` with `intValue()`, adds in primitive `int`, boxes the result with `Integer.valueOf(int)`, and `return j` unboxes again. Three method calls hide in one innocent line. Two rules follow immediately:

- Unboxing calls a method on the reference. If the reference is `null`, you get a `NullPointerException` even though your source shows no `.`.
- Boxing calls `valueOf`, which may allocate a new object. Where it allocates, and where it reuses an existing one, is the source of the identity puzzles below.

Use `Integer.valueOf(int)` (or let autoboxing do it), never `new Integer(5)`. The constructors of all wrappers have been deprecated since Java 9 and marked for removal since Java 16; they always allocate a fresh object and defeat the cache.

### The Integer cache and the == trap

`==` on two references compares **identity** (are they the same object?), not value. For wrappers that is almost never what you want. But a cache makes it appear to work sometimes, which is worse than never working. `Integer.valueOf(int)` keeps a pre-built array of `Integer` objects for -128 to 127 and hands out the same instance every time; outside that range it allocates a new one. The Java Language Specification requires this caching for boxing of small values, so the behaviour is guaranteed, not an implementation accident. Run the following program, which also covers the other traps in this chapter:

blocks.title: Boxing.java

blocks.code:
$ java Boxing.java
127 == 127 : true
128 == 128 : false
128 equals : true
valueOf(1000) == : false
Long 127 == : true
Long 128 == : false
Character 'a' == : true
Boolean == : true
Double 1.0 == : false
Integer vs Long equals : false
Integer == int : true
after remove(1)            : [10, 30, 1]
after remove(Integer 1)    : [10, 30]
NPE unboxing a missing map value
NPE from ternary with int operand
both boxed: null
x=11 y=10
mixed ternary: 1.0
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `127 == 127` is `true` and `128 == 128` is `false`. Both use autoboxing; only the first lands in the cache. `equals` compares values and is always right.
- `Double` has no cache, so `Double.valueOf(1.0) == Double.valueOf(1.0)` is `false`. `Boolean` and the small `Character` and `Byte` values are always shared.
- `Integer == int` (the line `c == 128`) is a **numeric** comparison: when one operand is a primitive, the other is unboxed and the values are compared. That is the safe form.
- `Integer.valueOf(5).equals(Long.valueOf(5))` is `false`: `equals` first checks that the other object is an `Integer`. Comparing different wrapper types never succeeds.
- `x++` on an `Integer` is `x = Integer.valueOf(x.intValue() + 1)`: a **new** object is assigned to `x`. `y` still points to the old one, as immutability promises.

#### The cache range is tunable

The lower bound -128 is fixed. The upper bound is 127 by default, but the JVM flag `-XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=<n>` (or the system property `java.lang.Integer.IntegerCache.high`) raises it. Re-running the first lines with `java` `-XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=1000 Boxing.java` changes the second line:

blocks.code:
$ java -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=1000 Boxing.java
127 == 127 : true
128 == 128 : true
128 equals : true
blocks.title: Same code, different answer

blocks.text: This is the strongest argument for never using `==` on boxed values: code that "works" in your tests may break when a flag or a value changes. Lint rules (SonarQube, Error Prone, IDE inspections) flag it for the same reason.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why does `Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b` give true but `Integer c = 128, d = 128; c == d` give false? `Integer.valueOf` caches instances for -128 to 127, so boxing both 127s returns the same object and `==` (reference comparison) is true. 128 is outside the default cache, so two separate objects are created. The fix is `equals` (or unboxing: `c.intValue() == d.intValue()`). The cache upper bound can be changed with `-XX:AutoBoxCacheMax`, which is one more reason never to depend on it.

### NullPointerException from unboxing

Because unboxing calls `xxxValue()`, any place where a `null` wrapper meets a primitive context throws. The three common sources are in the program above:

- **Map lookups.** `Map.get` returns `null` for a missing key, and `int n = stock.get("ink")` unboxes it. Use `getOrDefault("ink", 0)`, or check `containsKey`, or keep the value as `Integer` and test it for `null`.
- **Mixed ternaries.** In `flag ? 1 : (Integer) null`, one operand is a primitive `int` and the other an `Integer`. The ternary's rules make the result type `int` (binary numeric promotion), so the `null` is unboxed whenever it is chosen. If both operands are wrapper types, as in `flag ? Integer.valueOf(1) : null`, no unboxing happens and the result is simply `null`.
- **Fields and returns.** An `Integer` field that was never set is `null`, and `return count;` from a method declared `int` unboxes it. Database columns that are nullable map naturally to wrapper fields, so this shows up often in entity classes.

The last line of the output, `mixed ternary: 1.0`, shows a quieter ternary rule. When both operands of `?:` are convertible to numbers, the result type is the promoted numeric type, so `true ? Integer.valueOf(1) :` `Double.valueOf(2.0)` unboxes the `Integer` and widens it to `double`, printing `1.0`, not `1`.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Overloads and boxing interact. `list.remove(1)` on a `List<Integer>` removes the element at **index** 1, because `remove(int index)` is an exact match and wins before any boxing is considered. To remove the **value** 1 you must write `list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1))`. The output above shows both results.

### Performance cost of boxing

A primitive `int` takes 4 bytes. An `Integer` is an object: a header plus the value, typically 16 bytes on a 64-bit HotSpot JVM with compressed references, and a `List<Integer>` also stores a 4-byte reference to each (the object layout chapter in Part 9 gives the numbers). So a `List<Integer>` of a million numbers needs roughly four times the memory of an `int[]`, and traversing it chases pointers to scattered objects instead of reading a contiguous block, which is slow for the CPU cache. In a hot loop each boxing operation may also allocate, creating garbage for the collector.

The classic demonstration accumulates into a `Long` instead of a `long`:

On the build machine (typical, measured with `System.nanoTime`, one run each, no benchmarking harness) the first loop took about 2.2 seconds and the second about 2.7 seconds. The gap here is smaller than folklore suggests, because the JIT compiler can sometimes remove the allocation (escape analysis); on other machines, JVMs or less simple loops the boxed version can be many times slower. Treat these figures as a hint, not a benchmark; the reliable rules are structural:

- Use primitives for local variables, loop counters, accumulators, and fields that can never be absent.
- Use wrappers only when you need an object: generics, collections, `Optional<Integer>`, nullable database values.
- For large numeric collections consider primitive streams (`IntStream`) and arrays, or specialised libraries, instead of `List<Integer>`. The streams chapter in Part 7 shows `mapToInt` for exactly this reason.

### The Number hierarchy and parsing

`java.lang.Number` is an abstract class. Six wrappers extend it (`Byte`, `Short`, `Integer`, `Long`, `Float`, `Double`), and so do `BigInteger`, `BigDecimal` and the atomic classes `AtomicInteger` and `AtomicLong`. `Character` and `Boolean` do **not**: they extend `Object` directly. `Number` declares the conversions `intValue()`, `longValue()`, `floatValue()`, `doubleValue()` (plus `byteValue()` and `shortValue()`); they truncate or narrow exactly like a cast, so `Number n = 3.99; n.intValue()` is `3`.

blocks.title: Nums.java

blocks.code:
$ java Nums.java
Integer extends Number, Number? true
Double extends Number, Number? true
BigDecimal extends Number, Number? true
BigInteger extends Number, Number? true
AtomicInteger extends Number, Number? true
Character extends Object, Number? false
Boolean extends Object, Number? false
3 3 3.99
43
43
101010 ff 255
-1 -1 5 2147483647 4
For input string: "12x"
1 true false
true false
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text: Two points are worth remembering. First, `parseInt(String)` returns a primitive `int` and `valueOf(String)` returns an `Integer` (through the cache); use `parseInt` when you want a number to compute with. Both throw the unchecked `NumberFormatException` for bad input, so validate or catch it when parsing user data. Second, the last two lines show that `Double.equals` and `==` disagree. `equals` follows the bit pattern, so `Double.valueOf(Double.NaN).equals(Double.NaN)` is `true` and `0.0` is not equal to `-0.0`, which keeps `HashMap` lookups consistent. The `==` operator follows IEEE 754, where `NaN != NaN` and `0.0 == -0.0`. Use `Double.compare` when you need a total ordering (for sorting) and mind that `==` on primitive doubles is a numeric comparison.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Prefer the static helpers over hand-written logic: `Integer.compare(a, b)` instead of `a - b` (which overflows), `Integer.sum`, `Integer.max`, `Integer.toString(n, radix)`, `Long.parseLong`, `Character.isLetter`, `Boolean.parseBoolean`. For money and exact decimals use `BigDecimal`, not `Double`, as the type-conversion chapter explained.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In Spring and JPA code, entity ids and nullable columns are usually `Long` or `Integer` (so that "not saved yet" can be `null`), while counters and flags inside business logic are primitives. A very common production bug is `if` `(order.getId() == otherOrder.getId())` on two `Long` ids: it works in tests with small ids and silently fails once ids pass 127. Use `Objects.equals(a, b)` or `.equals`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Every primitive has an immutable wrapper; autoboxing is compiler-inserted `valueOf` and `xxxValue()` calls.
- `==` on wrappers compares identity. Only -128 to 127 (and `Boolean`, small `Character`) are cached, so always compare with `equals`, or unbox with a primitive.
- Unboxing `null` throws `NullPointerException`: watch map lookups, mixed ternaries and nullable fields.
- Boxing costs memory, indirection and garbage; use primitives for arithmetic and wrappers only where an object is required.
- `Number` is the abstract parent of the numeric wrappers, big numbers and atomics; `Character` and `Boolean` are not `Number`s.

Knowing the syntax of classes, interfaces, enums and records is the easy half. The harder half is deciding what to build with them: which things become classes, which depend on which, and how to leave room for change without paying for flexibility you never use. Bad class design rarely fails on day one. It fails six months later when a small requirement forces edits in twelve files, or when a bug appears because two parts of the program shared a mutable object. This chapter gathers the design habits that matter most in everyday Java, each with a small example you can run, and finishes with a checklist you can apply in code reviews and interviews.

### Composition over inheritance

Inheritance (`extends`) is the strongest coupling Java offers. A subclass depends on the superclass's **implementation**, not only its public contract: which methods call which, in what order, and what they assume. When the superclass changes, subclasses can break even though no signature changed. **Composition** means building a class by holding another object in a field and forwarding calls to it. The class depends only on the other object's public methods.

The classic demonstration is a set that counts how many elements were ever added. The inheritance version looks natural; the composition version is correct:

blocks.title: Fragile.java

blocks.code:
$ java Fragile.java
inheritance: expected 3, got 6
composition: expected 3, got 3
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The inheritance version counts every element twice. Its `addAll` adds `c.size()` and then calls `super.addAll`, and `HashSet`'s inherited `addAll` is implemented by calling the overridden `add` for each element, which increments the counter again. Nothing in the documentation promised that, and a future JDK could change it either way. This is the **fragile base class problem**.

The rules of thumb:

- Use inheritance only for a true "is-a" relationship, when the subclass honours everything the superclass promises, and when the superclass was designed for extension (documented, or abstract).
- Otherwise hold the collaborator in a `private final` field. Composition lets you swap the collaborator (pass a `TreeSet` instead), test with a fake, and hide the inner type from callers.
- Share behaviour between unrelated classes with an interface (with `default` methods if useful) and a helper object, not a deep class tree. If you do not intend a class to be extended, make it `final` (as the wrapper classes and `String` are); the "design for inheritance or prohibit it" rule from *Effective Java* is sound advice.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why is "favour composition over inheritance" a common design guideline? Inheritance couples a subclass to the superclass's implementation details (fragile base class) and fixes the relationship at compile time. Composition depends only on a public contract, can be changed at run time by passing a different collaborator, and is easier to test. Use inheritance for genuine is-a relationships designed for extension, and composition for reuse.

### SOLID in plain Java

SOLID is five guidelines for class design, popularised by Robert C. Martin. They are guidelines, not laws: applying them mechanically produces needless interfaces. Used with judgement they keep code easy to change. Here is each one with a Java illustration.

#### S: Single Responsibility

A class should have one reason to change. A class `OrderService` that also formats invoices as PDF, talks to SQL and sends email will change whenever any of those change. Split by responsibility: one class for the business rule, one for persistence, one for notification.

#### O and D: Open/Closed and Dependency Inversion

Software entities should be **open for extension, closed for modification**: add behaviour by adding code (a new class), not by editing a working `if`/`switch` chain. **Dependency inversion** says high-level logic should depend on abstractions (interfaces), not on concrete low-level classes, and receive its collaborators from outside (constructor injection). Together they give you this shape, which is the core idea behind Spring's dependency injection:

blocks.title: Solid.java

blocks.code:
$ java Solid.java
saved Order[id=A1, total=99.5]
Order A1 placed
Percent[pct=10.0] -> 180.0
Flat[off=25.0] -> 175.0
Flat[off=500.0] -> 0.0
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
`OrderService` has no idea whether the repository is a database or a list, nor whether notifications are email or a log line: in production you pass real implementations, in a unit test two lambdas (both interfaces have one method, so lambdas fit). Adding a `BuyOneGetOne` discount requires a new record and no change to existing code. If you know the sealed types from the previous chapters, note the trade-off: a **sealed** `Discount` makes adding a variant a deliberate, compiler-checked edit everywhere it is handled (closed for extension, open for new operations), while an open interface does the opposite. Choose by which kind of change you expect.

#### L: Liskov Substitution

Code that works with a base type must keep working with any subtype. Subtypes may not strengthen preconditions or weaken the promises of the base. The standard counter-example is a `Square` that extends a mutable `Rectangle`:

blocks.title: Lsp.java

blocks.code:
$ java Lsp.java
expected 10, got 10
expected 10, got 4
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Mathematically a square is a rectangle, but a *mutable* square does not honour the contract "width and height change independently". The fix is not cleverer code but a different model: make shapes immutable values (a `Shape` interface with `area()`; separate `Rectangle` and `Square` records), so nobody can observe the broken promise. Other Liskov violations to avoid: an override that throws `UnsupportedOperationException` for an inherited method, and an override that returns or accepts narrower values than documented.

#### I: Interface Segregation

Prefer several small interfaces to one large one, so a class is never forced to implement methods it does not need. `Comparable`, `Runnable`, `Iterable` and `AutoCloseable` are one-method interfaces for exactly this reason, and a class can implement as many as it needs. A 15-method `DataStore` interface that every fake has to implement fully is a smell.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Do not create an interface for every class "just in case". One implementation and no prospect of another is a reason to skip the interface. Introduce one when you have a second implementation, a need to substitute in tests, or a module boundary to protect.

### Immutability checklist

An **immutable** object cannot change after construction. Immutable objects can be shared freely between threads and callers with no locking, are safe as `HashMap` keys and `HashSet` elements, and cannot be left in a half-updated state. `String`, the wrappers, `BigDecimal` and the `java.time` types are immutable, and so are records (shallowly, as the records chapter explained). To write your own class:

1. Declare the class `final` (or give it only private constructors) so a subclass cannot add mutability.
2. Make all fields `private final`.
3. Provide no setters or other mutators. "Change" operations return a new object (a "wither": `loan.withDue(...)`).
4. Initialise every field in the constructor, validating arguments there, so the object is never visible in an invalid state.
5. **Defensive copy** every mutable argument on the way in, and every mutable field on the way out (or expose only an unmodifiable view).
6. Do not let `this` escape from the constructor (do not register `this` as a listener or start a thread in it).

The following program applies the checklist by hand and shows what a record does and does not do for you:

blocks.title: Imm.java

blocks.code:
$ java Imm.java
[fragile spine]
UOE
2026-11-01 -> 2026-11-15
[a, b] vs [a]
true true
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text: What to notice: the caller's later `n.add("late once")` did not leak into `loan` because the constructor copied the list. `List.copyOf` returns an unmodifiable list, so even `loan.notes().add(...)` fails. The `LeakyLoan` record saw the caller's later change (`[a, b]`) because a record stores the reference it is given; the compact constructor in `SafeLoan` fixed it with one line. `List.copyOf` (Java 10) has a bonus: if the argument is already an immutable list from `List.of`, it returns it without copying.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: `final` on a field makes the *reference* constant, not the object behind it. A `private final List<String> notes` can still be mutated through `notes.add(...)` unless the list itself is unmodifiable. Immutability is a property of the whole object graph reachable from the fields.

### equals and hashCode: let records do it

Hand-written `equals`/`hashCode` is easy to get wrong (the Object class chapter showed how a missing `hashCode` breaks `HashMap`). For classes that are plain **values** (a point, money, a customer id, a library loan), make them records: the compiler generates `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` from all components, consistently and with no maintenance as fields change. Two cautions. Records compare components with `equals`, so an array component is compared by identity; use a `List` instead. And do not make an object with identity (a bank account whose balance changes, a JPA entity with a generated id) a record: two accounts with the same balance are not the same account. Mutable entities keep an explicit `equals` based on a stable business key or id, or they inherit identity equality, which is fine when two distinct objects should never be equal.

If you do write `equals` by hand, the safe recipe on a final class is: check `this == o`, check the type (`o instanceof Loan` `other`, or `getClass()` if the class is extensible), compare fields with `Objects.equals` (or `Double.compare` for floats), and compute `hashCode` from exactly the same fields using `Objects.hash(...)`.

### API design smells

Classes are used by other people (and by you in three months). Common smells, with the fix:

rows: Named options type, an enum, or two methods with clear names.
A record or builder grouping related values.
`Optional<T>` for a single result, an empty collection for many. Never return `null` for a collection.
Magic ints and strings for modes
Public mutable fields or exposed internal lists
Private fields, copies or unmodifiable views, behaviour methods instead of getters and setters.
Setters that allow a partly built object
Constructor or builder that produces a valid object in one step.
Class that is "data plus a manager" (an `OrderUtil` full of static methods acting on a passive `Order`)
Put behaviour with the data it uses (the "tell, do not ask" idea).
The most specific type; generics instead of casts.
blocks.caption: Smells in class and method design.

blocks.text: Here the first three smells are fixed in a few lines. Notice that the "before" version compiles and returns `null` to the caller:

blocks.title: Smells.java

blocks.code:
$ java Smells.java
Report[title=Sales as PDF]
none
null
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The call `make("Q", true, false, 2)` is unreadable (what is `2`? which boolean is colour?) and silently returned `null`; the call `make("Sales", Options.defaults().withLandscape())` states its intent. A tip learned the hard way: a record accessor already uses the component name (`landscape()`), so a method that builds a modified copy cannot reuse that name; the convention is `withLandscape()`.

### A short checklist for a new class

- Can I state what this class is for in one sentence, with no "and"?
- Is every field `private`, and `final` unless there is a reason? Could this be a record or an enum?
- Does the constructor leave the object valid? Are arguments validated and mutable ones copied?
- Do callers depend on an interface or on this concrete type? Do I take my dependencies through the constructor?
- Is it `final` or documented for extension? If it extends something, is it really an is-a and does it honour the parent's contract?
- Are `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString` consistent and complete (or generated)?
- Could a caller misuse it with a `null`, a negative number, or the wrong call order? Can I make that impossible in the types?

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In a Spring Boot service these ideas show up everywhere: services receive repositories and clients through constructor injection (dependency inversion), request and response bodies are records (immutable DTOs), entities use identity equality or an id-based `equals`, and "enum instead of a string status" prevents a class of data bugs. Reviewers routinely reject long boolean-flag methods and `return null` for collections.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Prefer composition to inheritance; inherit only for a real is-a relationship in a class designed for extension, otherwise make the class `final`.
- Depend on small interfaces and receive collaborators through the constructor (SOLID: single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion).
- Immutability checklist: final class, private final fields, no mutators, validate in the constructor, defensive copies in and out.
- Use records for plain values so `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` are generated; keep identity-based equality for mutable entities.
- Avoid API smells: boolean flags, long parameter lists, null returns, magic constants and exposed internals.
#### Classes and Objects

items.question: What does this print, and why? `Book a = new Book("X"); Book b = a; b = new Book("Y");` `System.out.println(a == b);` (assume `Book` has the constructor shown above).
items.answer: It prints `false`. `b` was repointed at a new object; `a` still refers to the first one.

items.question: A class has no constructors. Another programmer adds `Book(String t)`. Existing code `new Book()` stops compiling. Why?
items.answer: The compiler only supplies the default no-argument constructor when the class declares no constructor. Declaring any constructor removes it.

items.question: In `InitOrder`, why did `Derived.show` print `name=null` even though the field is assigned `"set"`?
items.answer: The superclass constructor called the overridden `show()` before the subclass field initialisers ran, so the fields still held default values.

items.question: What is wrong here? `class T { int a = b; int b = 2; }`
items.answer: Illegal forward reference: `a`'s initialiser reads `b` before `b` is declared. It is a compile-time error.

items.question: Does reading `Config.MAX` (a `static final int MAX = 10;`) run the static block of `Config`? What if the field is `static final int MAX = compute();`?
items.answer: No for a compile-time constant (the value is inlined, the class is not initialised). Yes for `compute()`: the class initialises on first access.

items.question: Can a Java method change which object the caller's variable refers to? Explain with the `replace` method from `Refs`.
items.answer: No. The method gets a copy of the reference. Reassigning the parameter changes only the copy; mutating the object it points to is visible to the caller.

blocks.text: #### Static, Access Control and Packages

items.question: What is the difference between a static field and an instance field? Which one is stored once per object?
items.answer: A static field exists once per class and is shared by all objects; an instance field exists once per object.

items.question: Why does this fail to compile? `public class A { int n; public static void main(String[] a) { n = 1; } }`
items.answer: `main` is static and has no `this`, so it cannot access the instance field `n` without an object.

items.question: A class in package `p1` has a package-private method. Can a subclass in package `p2` override it? Can code in `p1` call it?
items.answer: No: package-private members are not visible outside `p1`, so a `p2` method with that signature is a new method, not an override. Yes, code in `p1` can call it.

items.question: What does this print? `final int[] a = {1}; a[0] = 2; System.out.println(a[0]);` Does `final` stop it?
items.answer: It prints `2`. `final` only prevents reassigning `a`; the array contents can change.

items.question: Name two things that break the immutability of a class whose fields are all `private final`.
items.answer: Storing a mutable object passed in by the caller without copying it, and returning a reference to an internal mutable object (also: a non-final class that a subclass can make mutable).

items.question: Why is `setBalance(double)` a poor method on a bank account class? What would you offer instead?
items.answer: It lets any caller bypass the rules (overdraft limits, auditing). Offer `deposit` and `withdraw`, which validate and keep the balance consistent.

blocks.text: #### Inheritance

items.question: What does this print? `class A { A() { System.out.print("A"); } } class B extends A { B() {` `System.out.print("B"); } } new B();`
items.answer: `AB`. The superclass constructor runs first (implicit `super()`), then the subclass constructor body.

items.question: Why does `class Parent { Parent(int x) {} } class Child extends Parent { }` not compile?
items.answer: `Child` has the implicit default constructor, which calls `super()`, but `Parent` has no no-argument constructor. `Child` needs an explicit constructor calling `super(someInt)`.

items.question: Can a subclass override `public Object get()` with `String get()`? With `private Object get()`? Explain.
items.answer: Yes to `String get()`: covariant return types are allowed. No to `private`: access cannot be weaker than `public`.

items.question: What does this print? `class P { static String s() { return "P"; } } class C extends P { static String` `s() { return "C"; } } P p = new C(); System.out.println(p.s());`
items.answer: It prints `P`: static methods are hidden, and the declared type `P` decides.

items.question: Why is `class Stack extends ArrayList` considered bad design even though it compiles and works?
items.answer: It exposes methods like `add(index, e)` and `remove(index)` that break stack semantics, and it ties the class to `ArrayList` forever. A stack should contain a list (composition).

items.question: What is the fragile base class problem?
items.answer: A subclass depends on implementation details of its parent, so a harmless-looking change in the parent breaks the subclass.

blocks.text: #### Polymorphism and Dynamic Dispatch

items.question: What is the difference between the static type and the dynamic type of `Animal a = new Dog();`?
items.answer: Static: `Animal`, known to the compiler from the declaration. Dynamic: `Dog`, the real class of the object, known only at run time.

items.question: What does this print? `static void f(Object o){System.out.print("O");} static void f(String` `s){System.out.print("S");} ... Object x = "hi"; f(x); f("hi"); f(null);`
items.answer: `OSS`. The first call uses static type `Object`; for `f(null)` the most specific applicable overload is `String`.

items.question: Why does a class with `public boolean equals(Point p)` not work in a `HashSet<Point>`? What one-word fix prevents the mistake?
items.answer: It overloads instead of overriding `equals(Object)`, and `HashSet` calls the latter. `@Override` makes the compiler reject it.

items.question: Which of `a.name`, `a.sound()`, `a.greet(d)` (from `Dispatch`) are resolved at run time?
items.answer: Only `a.sound()` (an overridden instance method). The field read and the overload choice are decided at compile time.

items.question: When does a downcast throw `ClassCastException`, and how do you avoid it?
items.answer: When the object's real class is not the target type or a subclass. Test first with `instanceof` (ideally the pattern form), or redesign so the cast is unnecessary.

items.question: Which JVM instruction is used for a call to a `private` method, and why does it need no dispatch?
items.answer: `invokespecial`: a private method cannot be overridden, so the target is known at compile time.

blocks.text: #### Abstract Classes and Interfaces

items.question: Can an abstract class have a constructor? If you cannot call `new` on it, what is it for?
items.answer: Yes. A subclass constructor calls it with `super(...)` to initialise the shared state. The class exists to be extended.

items.question: What does `new X().hi()` return if `X implements A, B`, with `B extends A` and both defining `default String hi()`?
items.answer: `B`'s version: the most specific interface wins.

items.question: This does not compile; what is wrong? `interface P { default void go() {} } interface Q { default void` `go() {} } class R implements P, Q { }`
items.answer: `R` inherits two unrelated defaults for `go()`. It must override `go()`, for example calling `P.super.go()`.

items.question: Are interface fields modifiable? What are `int MAX = 5;` modifiers inside an interface?
items.answer: No. They are implicitly `public static final`, so `MAX` is a constant.

items.question: Is `Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("x");` legal? Why?
items.answer: Yes: `Runnable` has one abstract method (`run`), so a lambda can implement it.

items.question: Give one reason to prefer an interface over an abstract class in a public API.
items.answer: A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class, and interfaces keep callers independent of any implementation (and make test doubles easy).

blocks.text: #### The Object Class

items.question: What does `System.out.println(new Object())` print, and which method produces it?
items.answer: Something like `java.lang.Object@659e0bfd` from `Object.toString`: class name, `@`, hex identity hash (varies per run).

items.question: A class overrides `equals(Object)` but not `hashCode()`. Name the concrete symptom in a `HashSet`.
items.answer: Equal objects usually land in different buckets, so `contains`, `remove` and `get` fail to find them and duplicates can be added.

items.question: What does this print? `BigDecimal a = new BigDecimal("2.0"), b = new BigDecimal("2.00");` `System.out.println(a.equals(b) + " " + a.compareTo(b));`
items.answer: `false 0`: `equals` compares scale as well as value, `compareTo` compares only numeric value.

items.question: Why must you not mutate a field used in `hashCode` after putting the object in a `HashMap` as a key?
items.answer: The entry stays in the bucket for the old hash; lookups now use the new hash and miss it. The entry is lost but still occupies memory.

items.question: `class Pt { int x; public boolean equals(Pt p) { return p != null && x == p.x; } }` is used as `Set<Pt>`. What is wrong, and what one annotation catches it?
items.answer: It overloads `equals(Pt)` instead of overriding `equals(Object)`, so the set uses identity equality. `@Override` makes the compiler reject it.

items.question: Why is `int[] b = a.clone();` acceptable while cloning ordinary objects is discouraged?
items.answer: Arrays have a well-defined, compiler-supported `clone` returning the right type; the problems of `Cloneable` (constructors, final fields, deep copy) do not apply to a flat array of primitives.

blocks.text: #### Nested, Inner, Local and Anonymous Classes

items.question: Which of the four nested kinds never has an outer-instance reference?
items.answer: The static nested class. (Local and anonymous classes created in a static method also have none.)

items.question: What is wrong with this code, and how do you fix it? `int n = 0; Runnable r = new Runnable() { public void` `run() { n++; } };`
items.answer: `n` is modified inside the class, so it is not effectively final and the code does not compile. Use an `AtomicInteger`, make the counter a field of an object, or restructure so the value is returned.

items.question: What does `Outer.this` mean inside an inner class, and how do you create an inner object from `main`?
items.answer: It is the enclosing instance of the inner object. From `main` you need an outer object: `Outer o = new Outer();` `Outer.Inner i = o.new Inner();`.

items.question: Why is a class file named `Outer$1.class` produced for an anonymous class?
items.answer: The JVM has no concept of nested classes; the compiler flattens each one into its own class file, naming anonymous classes `Outer$1`, `Outer$2` and so on.

items.question: Why can a long-lived anonymous object cause an `OutOfMemoryError` even if you no longer use the outer object?
items.answer: The inner object holds `this$0`, so everything reachable from the outer object stays reachable (here the 10 MB array) as long as the inner object is referenced.

items.question: What does `this` refer to inside a lambda versus inside an anonymous class body?
items.answer: In a lambda, `this` is the enclosing instance. In an anonymous class, `this` is the anonymous object itself.

blocks.text: #### Enums

items.question: What does `enum E { A, B }` compile to, and what are `A` and `B`?
items.answer: A final class `E extends Enum<E>` with two `public static final` instances `A` and `B`, created in a static initializer.

items.question: Is this legal? `new Level()` where `Level` is an enum.
items.answer: No. Enum constructors are private and you cannot instantiate an enum with `new`; the set of instances is closed.

items.question: What does this print? `enum T { X, Y, Z } ... System.out.println(T.Z.compareTo(T.X) + " " +` `T.valueOf("Y").ordinal());`
items.answer: `2 1`. `compareTo` returns the ordinal difference (2 - 0) and `Y` has ordinal 1.

items.question: Why is storing `ordinal()` in a database dangerous?
items.answer: Adding or reordering constants changes the ordinals, so stored numbers then point at the wrong constants. Store the name or a stable code.

items.question: When would you pick `EnumMap` over `HashMap`, and what must you pass to its constructor?
items.answer: When keys are an enum: it is faster and smaller (an array indexed by ordinal) and iterates in declaration order. Pass the key type's `Class` object, e.g. `new EnumMap<>(Day.class)`.

items.question: Why does `Level.valueOf("high")` fail when the constant is `HIGH`, and what is thrown?
items.answer: `valueOf` matches the name exactly and is case-sensitive; it throws `IllegalArgumentException` ("No enum constant ...").

blocks.text: #### Records

items.question: Name five members the compiler generates for `record Point(int x, int y) {}`.
items.answer: Private final fields `x`, `y`; the canonical constructor; accessors `x()`, `y()`; `equals`; `hashCode`; `toString`.

items.question: In a compact constructor, why does `this.x = x;` fail to compile, and how do you change the stored value?
items.answer: In a compact constructor the fields are assigned automatically at the end, so assigning them yourself is an error. To change the stored value, reassign the parameter: `x = Math.abs(x);`.

items.question: What does this print? `record R(int[] a) {} ... System.out.println(new R(new int[]{1}).equals(new R(new` `int[]{1})));`
items.answer: `false`. Arrays use identity `equals`, and the record's `equals` delegates to it for that component.

items.question: Why does a non-canonical record constructor have to start with `this(...)`?
items.answer: So that every construction path goes through the canonical constructor, and therefore through its validation and field assignment.

items.question: A record has a `List<String>` component. How do you make the record safe against a caller who later mutates their list?
items.answer: Copy it in the compact constructor: `items = List.copyOf(items);` (this also rejects `null` elements), and do not expose a mutable list from accessors.

items.question: Why should you not use a record as a JPA `@Entity`?
items.answer: Entities need mutable state, a no-argument constructor and non-final classes (for lazy-loading proxies); a record is final, immutable and has no no-arg constructor. Use records for DTOs and projections instead.

blocks.text: #### Sealed Classes and Interfaces

items.question: What three modifiers may a permitted subclass of a sealed class use?
items.answer: `final`, `sealed` or `non-sealed` (records and enums count as implicitly final).

items.question: When can the `permits` clause be left out?
items.answer: When all permitted subtypes are declared in the same compilation unit (file), or are nested inside the sealed type; the compiler infers them.

items.question: What is wrong with this? `sealed interface S permits A {} record A() implements S {} class B implements` `S {}`
items.answer: `B` is not in the `permits` list, so the compiler rejects it ("class is not allowed to extend sealed class").

items.question: Why does a switch over a sealed type not need a `default`, and what is the risk of adding one anyway?
items.answer: Because the compiler knows all subtypes, it can verify every case is covered. A `default` would hide a missing new variant until it fails at runtime.

items.question: A sealed interface is implemented by three records. Is the product or the sum type the interface? And the records?
items.answer: The interface is the sum type (one of several alternatives); each record is a product type (several fields together).

items.question: Does `non-sealed` break the exhaustiveness guarantee? Explain briefly.
items.answer: No. The `non-sealed` subtype is itself still one of the known permitted variants, so the switch covers it by its own case; you just cannot know the types below it.

blocks.text: #### Pattern Matching

items.question: What does this print? `Object o = "hi"; if (!(o instanceof String s)) { System.out.println("no");` `return; } System.out.println(s.length());`
items.answer: `2`. The binding `s` is in scope after the early return because reaching it means the test succeeded.

items.question: Why does this not compile? `switch (o) { case CharSequence c -> ..; case String s -> ..; default -> ..;` `}`
items.answer: `case String s` is dominated: every `String` is a `CharSequence`, so it can never be reached. Put the more specific case first.

items.question: How do you make a pattern switch accept `null` without an exception?
items.answer: Add `case null ->` (or `case null, default ->`). Otherwise a `null` selector throws `NullPointerException`.

items.question: What does `case Point(var x, var y) when x == y` do?
items.answer: It matches a `Point` and binds both components, and then only succeeds when the guard (the two coordinates are equal) is true; otherwise the next case is tried.

items.question: Is `null instanceof Object` true or false?
items.answer: False. `instanceof` never matches `null`.

items.question: Why do you not need `default` when every subtype of a sealed interface has a case?
items.answer: The compiler knows the permitted subtypes, so the cases are provably exhaustive. (An unexpected new subclass compiled later leads to a `MatchException` at runtime, which is why recompiling dependents matters.)

blocks.text: #### Wrapper Classes, Autoboxing and Identity

items.question: What does this print? `Integer a = 200, b = 200; System.out.println((a == b) + " " + a.equals(b) + " " +` `(a == 200));`
items.answer: `false true true`. 200 is outside the cache so `a == b` compares two different objects; `equals` compares values; `a` `== 200` unboxes `a`.

items.question: `Map<String, Integer> m = new HashMap<>(); int v = m.get("x");` throws. Which exception, and what are two ways to avoid it?
items.answer: `NullPointerException` (unboxing `null`). Use `m.getOrDefault("x", 0)`, or declare `Integer v` and test it for `null`, or check `containsKey` first.

items.question: What is the output? `List<Integer> l = new ArrayList<>(List.of(5, 6, 7)); l.remove(1);` `System.out.println(l);` How do you remove the value 6 instead?
items.answer: `[5, 7]`: `remove(1)` removes the element at index 1. Use `l.remove(Integer.valueOf(6))` to remove the value.

items.question: What does `Long.valueOf(7).equals(7)` return, and why?
items.answer: `false`. The argument `7` is boxed to `Integer`, and `Long.equals` returns `false` for any object that is not a `Long`.

items.question: What does `Object o = true ? 1 : 2.0; System.out.println(o);` print?
items.answer: `1.0`. One operand is `double`, so the ternary has type `double` and the `1` is widened.

items.question: Name two reasons to prefer `int` over `Integer` for a loop counter.
items.answer: A primitive avoids an allocation and a `valueOf` call each iteration, uses 4 bytes instead of an object, and can never be `null`, so it cannot throw on unboxing.

blocks.text: #### Designing Classes Well

items.question: Why does the `CountingHashSet` in this chapter report 6 for three elements?
items.answer: `addAll` adds `c.size()` and then `HashSet`'s inherited `addAll` calls the overridden `add` for each element, which counts them again.

items.question: A class has `private final List<String> items` and a getter `return items;`. Is it immutable? Give one fix.
items.answer: No: callers can modify the list through the getter. Return `List.copyOf(items)` or `Collections.unmodifiableList(items)`, and copy the list in the constructor too.

items.question: What is wrong with this record? `record Course(String name, String[] tags) {}` (hint: think of `equals`).
items.answer: A record compares components with `equals`, and arrays use identity, so two `Course` objects with equal tag contents are not equal and `hashCode` differs. Use `List<String>` (copied in a compact constructor).

items.question: A `Penguin` extends `Bird`, which has `fly()`. `Penguin.fly()` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. Which principle does this break, and what is a better design?
items.answer: Liskov Substitution: code that accepts a `Bird` cannot rely on `fly()`. Model flying separately (a `FlyingBird` interface or a capability), so only birds that fly promise it.

items.question: What does `new SafeLoan("Ravi", List.of("a")).equals(safe)` need to be true, and why did it work in this chapter?
items.answer: All components must be equal: the same member and equal notes. The compact constructor copied the list, and `List.equals` compares contents, so the lists with the same elements are equal.

items.question: Name two smells in `void export(String file, boolean zip, boolean overwrite, int type)`.
items.answer: Boolean flag parameters, a magic `int` mode, and a long parameter list. Use an options record and an enum.
